# Aviation and Plane Crash Statistics

Request Free Consultation

Despite air travel remaining the safest form of transportation, when [aviation accidents](https://www.aviationdisasterlaw.com/) do happen, the results are often catastrophic. There are no such things as minor airplane collisions or crash landings; these occurrences are devastating, life-altering events. Aviation accident rates have decreased in recent years, but the growing popularity of private jet travel and helicopter flights may soon reverse this trend.

In the United States, the [National Transportation Safety Board](https://www.ntsb.gov/Pages/home.aspx) (NTSB) tracks aviation accident statistics and investigates aviation disasters.

In 2007, the National Transportation Safety Board estimated a total of nearly 24 million flight hours. Of these 24 million hours, 6.84 of every 100,000 flight hours yielded an airplane crash, and 1.19 of every 100,000 yielded a fatal crash. This is down from an all-time high of 9.08 accidents per 100,000 hours in 1994. These numbers are higher for private flights, but private flights are much harder to document due to lax government regulation and non-reporting. [Private plane crashes](https://www.panish.law/private_plane_crash_attorneys.html) have been on the decline since the 1980s, but user error and insufficient training still contribute to many more accidents than are necessary each year.

![Image 13](https://www.panish.law/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/Aviation-and-Plane-Crash-Statistics-1024x540.jpg)

> _“Statistics show that up to 80 percent of all aviation accidents can be attributed to human error.”_

Statistics show that up to 80 percent of all aviation accidents can be attributed to human error. The most dangerous times include takeoff and landing, and the time periods before and after these events. Pilot error is thought to account for 53% of aircraft accidents, with mechanical failure (21%) and weather conditions (11%) following behind.

Even in the best training situations, where flight crews undertake comprehensive simulator-based training, human beings tend to revert to previous habitual behaviors. Training helps, but it takes people time to develop muscle memory, which can result in catastrophic unintended consequences, particularly when flying a highly maneuverable aircraft.

The NTSB database, which has records of every reportable accident since 2008, shows over 13 thousand accidents with at least one issue pertaining to personnel. All these accidents include over 20 thousand findings related to personnel, with an average of 1.54 per accident.

On the other hand, it’s important to note that other factors are always in play when pilot error occurs. The aircraft, environmental issues, and organizational issues are a few examples that may be taken into account if someone files a lawsuit for an accident.

## How Safe is Air Travel?

Compared to other major forms of transportation, with 0.04 deaths per 100 million miles traveled, train travel is much more dangerous than airplanes’ 0.01 deaths per 100 million miles. However, air travel is only as safe as the operator, the equipment, and the training procedures that underlie the flight itself. Without stringent aviation safety training and controls, air travel is unsafe for private and commercial passengers.

## Nearly Half of All Aviation Crashes Happen During Landing or Takeoff

One fact becomes clear after looking at historic aviation crash data and focusing on the phase of flight during which the crash took place: Landing and Takeoff are the most complex phases of flight for any airplane. Nearly half of all the aviation crashes we analyzed, covering the period 1983 – 201,9 took place during either landing or take-off procedures. These phases place a heavy load on airline crews and ground teams as well.

The tough combination of constant airplane configuration changes, having to navigate the plane, communicating with Air Traffic Control, and keeping an eye on ever-changing weather conditions increases the potential for unanticipated events, which sometimes lead to a crash.

## General Aviation Aircraft Involved in 78% of Crashes

Furthermore, our team analyzed the types of flights involved in the most crashes and found that general aviation aircraft were involved in almost 78% of all crashes. General aviation aircraft include all civilian flights except for passenger or cargo transport that is scheduled by an airline company.

![Image 16](https://www.panish.law/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/PSBR-Aviation-Crash-Statistics-3.png)

One of the main reasons why general aviation planes are involved in so many crashes is that there are many more of them flying than scheduled commercial flights.

However, if we look at the percentage of fatal accidents by the type of flight, we see that general aviation was involved in almost 45%, while non-US commercial and other flights share almost half of the crashes that involved a fatality.

# Aviation and Plane Crash Statistics

Request Free Consultation

Despite air travel remaining the safest form of transportation, when [aviation accidents](https://www.aviationdisasterlaw.com/) do happen, the results are often catastrophic. There are no such things as minor airplane collisions or crash landings; these occurrences are devastating, life-altering events. Aviation accident rates have decreased in recent years, but the growing popularity of private jet travel and helicopter flights may soon reverse this trend.

In the United States, the [National Transportation Safety Board](https://www.ntsb.gov/Pages/home.aspx) (NTSB) tracks aviation accident statistics and investigates aviation disasters.

In 2007, the National Transportation Safety Board estimated a total of nearly 24 million flight hours. Of these 24 million hours, 6.84 of every 100,000 flight hours yielded an airplane crash, and 1.19 of every 100,000 yielded a fatal crash. This is down from an all-time high of 9.08 accidents per 100,000 hours in 1994. These numbers are higher for private flights, but private flights are much harder to document due to lax government regulation and non-reporting. [Private plane crashes](https://www.panish.law/private_plane_crash_attorneys.html) have been on the decline since the 1980s, but user error and insufficient training still contribute to many more accidents than are necessary each year.

![Image 13](https://www.panish.law/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/Aviation-and-Plane-Crash-Statistics-1024x540.jpg)

> _“Statistics show that up to 80 percent of all aviation accidents can be attributed to human error.”_

Statistics show that up to 80 percent of all aviation accidents can be attributed to human error. The most dangerous times include takeoff and landing, and the time periods before and after these events. Pilot error is thought to account for 53% of aircraft accidents, with mechanical failure (21%) and weather conditions (11%) following behind.

Even in the best training situations, where flight crews undertake comprehensive simulator-based training, human beings tend to revert to previous habitual behaviors. Training helps, but it takes people time to develop muscle memory, which can result in catastrophic unintended consequences, particularly when flying a highly maneuverable aircraft.

The NTSB database, which has records of every reportable accident since 2008, shows over 13 thousand accidents with at least one issue pertaining to personnel. All these accidents include over 20 thousand findings related to personnel, with an average of 1.54 per accident.

On the other hand, it’s important to note that other factors are always in play when pilot error occurs. The aircraft, environmental issues, and organizational issues are a few examples that may be taken into account if someone files a lawsuit for an accident.

## How Safe is Air Travel?

Compared to other major forms of transportation, with 0.04 deaths per 100 million miles traveled, train travel is much more dangerous than airplanes’ 0.01 deaths per 100 million miles. However, air travel is only as safe as the operator, the equipment, and the training procedures that underlie the flight itself. Without stringent aviation safety training and controls, air travel is unsafe for private and commercial passengers.

## Nearly Half of All Aviation Crashes Happen During Landing or Takeoff

One fact becomes clear after looking at historic aviation crash data and focusing on the phase of flight during which the crash took place: Landing and Takeoff are the most complex phases of flight for any airplane. Nearly half of all the aviation crashes we analyzed, covering the period 1983 – 201,9 took place during either landing or take-off procedures. These phases place a heavy load on airline crews and ground teams as well.

The tough combination of constant airplane configuration changes, having to navigate the plane, communicating with Air Traffic Control, and keeping an eye on ever-changing weather conditions increases the potential for unanticipated events, which sometimes lead to a crash.

## General Aviation Aircraft Involved in 78% of Crashes

Furthermore, our team analyzed the types of flights involved in the most crashes and found that general aviation aircraft were involved in almost 78% of all crashes. General aviation aircraft include all civilian flights except for passenger or cargo transport that is scheduled by an airline company.

![Image 16](https://www.panish.law/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/PSBR-Aviation-Crash-Statistics-3.png)

One of the main reasons why general aviation planes are involved in so many crashes is that there are many more of them flying than scheduled commercial flights.

However, if we look at the percentage of fatal accidents by the type of flight, we see that general aviation was involved in almost 45%, while non-US commercial and other flights share almost half of the crashes that involved a fatality.

![Image 17](https://www.panish.law/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/PSBR-Aviation-Crash-Statistics-4.png)

### Below is a year-by-year summary of commercial airplane crashes from 2022 through early 2026 highlights major incidents around the world involving passenger jets, regional aircraft, cargo planes, and charter operations.

## 2026 Commercial Airplane Crashes: (Up To Date)

### **January 2026:**

*   An Indonesian Air Transport ATR 42-512, operating on behalf of the Directorate General of Marine and Fisheries Resources Surveillance, crashed in Sulawesi while flying from Yogyakarta to Makassar. All 10 occupants were killed.
*   SATENA Flight 8849, a Beechcraft 1900D flying from Cúcuta to Ocaña, Colombia, crashed in Curasica, Playa de Belén. All 15 people on board died.

### **Febraury 2026:**

*   An Embraer EMB 110 Bandeirante operated by Agape Flights on a domestic cargo flight crashed en route, killing both occupants.

### **March 2026:**

*   Air Canada Express Flight 8646, a Bombardier CRJ-900 operated by Jazz Aviation, collided with a fire truck while landing at LaGuardia Airport, resulting in two fatalities—the captain and co-pilot. This incident marks the first fatal crash involving a CRJ-900 aircraft.

## 2025 Commercial Airplane Crashes:

### **January 2025:**

*   An Airbus A321-200 operating as Air Busan Flight 391, bound for Hong Kong from Busan, caught fire just before takeoff at Gimhae International Airport. All 176 passengers and crew survived, though seven sustained injuries.
*   A Beechcraft 1900 operated by Light Air Services, transporting oil workers, crashed shortly after departing from GPOC Unity Airstrip in South Sudan. Of the 21 people onboard, only one survived.
*   During the 2025 Potomac River mid-air collision, American Eagle Flight 5342, a Bombardier CRJ700 operated by PSA Airlines, collided with a US Army Sikorsky UH-60L helicopter over the Potomac River. The accident resulted in the deaths of all 64 people on the CRJ700 and all three aboard the UH-60L.
*   Med Jets Flight 056, a Learjet 55 operated by Jet Rescue Air Ambulance, crashed in Philadelphia’s Castor Gardens neighborhood shortly after takeoff. There were no survivors.

### **February 2025:**

*   Bering Air Flight 445, a Cessna 208B Grand Caravan en route from Unalakleet to Nome, Alaska, vanished over Norton Sound. The wreckage was found the next day, confirming the deaths of all 10 onboard.
*   Delta Connection Flight 4819, a Bombardier CRJ-900, crash-landed at Toronto Pearson International Airport. While all 76 passengers and four crew members survived, 18 sustained injuries.

### **March 2025:**

*   Lanhsa Flight 018, a British Aerospace Jetstream 32, crashed into the sea after overrunning the runway during takeoff from Roatán Airport. Thirteen of the 18 people on board lost their lives.
*   A Trident Aviation DHC-5 cargo plane crashed in a field near Mogadishu, Somalia, following a technical failure, resulting in the deaths of all five people on board.

### **April 2025:**

*   Tropic Air Flight 711, a Cessna 208B Grand Caravan EX, was hijacked during a flight from Corozal to San Pedro. Due to low fuel, the pilot was forced to make an emergency landing in Belize City. Upon landing, the hijacker injured three of the 15 other people on board before being shot and killed by an armed passenger.

### **May 2025:**

*   Air Panamá Flight 982, a Fokker 50 carrying 38 people, crashed after veering off Runway 27 during landing at Bocas Del Toro Airport (BOC/MPBO) on Colón Island, Panama. Of the 3 crew members and 35 passengers onboard, 12 were injured, but all survived the accident.

### **June 2025:**

*   Air India Flight 171, a Boeing 787-8 en route from Ahmedabad to London Gatwick, crashed into a medical college building shortly after takeoff. The accident claimed the lives of 241 out of 242 passengers and crew, as well as 19 people on the ground. It was the first fatal crash and total loss of a Boeing 787 aircraft.
*   A hot air balloon operated by Sobrevoar caught fire mid-flight and crashed near Praia Grande, Brazil. Eight of the 21 people on board lost their lives.

### **July 2025:**

*   On July 24, Angara Airlines Flight 2311, an Antonov An-24 traveling from Ignatyevo Airport to Tynda Airport, crashed into a mountain during its approach to Tynda, Russia, killing all 42 passengers and six crew members on board.

### **October 2025:**

*   Emirates SkyCargo Flight 9788, a Boeing 747-400BDSF, struck an airport maintenance vehicle and veered off the runway while landing at Hong Kong International Airport, resulting in the deaths of two people in the ground vehicle.
*   Mombasa Air Safari Flight 203, a Cessna 208B Grand Caravan on a domestic route from Ukunda to Kichwa, crashed near Kwale, Kenya, killing all 11 people aboard.

### **November 2025:**

*   UPS Airlines Flight 2976, a McDonnell Douglas MD-11F operating from Louisville, Kentucky to Honolulu, Hawaii, crashed shortly after takeoff, killing 14 people and injuring 15 others.
*   An AirJet Angola Embraer ERJ-145 crashed at Kolwezi Airport in the DRC; all 29 people on board survived.

## 2024 Commercial Airplane Crashes:

### **January 2024:**

*   The 2024 Haneda Airport runway collision involved Japan Airlines Flight 516, an Airbus A350 from New Chitose Airport, colliding with a Japan Coast Guard De Havilland Canada Dash 8 aircraft during landing. While all 379 occupants of the Japan Airlines flight were evacuated safely, tragically, five of the six occupants aboard the Coast Guard aircraft lost their lives.
*   Alaska Airlines Flight 1282, a Boeing 737 MAX 9 departing from Portland International Airport, experienced uncontrolled decompression when a plug covering an unused exit door blew out. Despite the harrowing incident, the aircraft made a safe return to Portland with all 177 passengers and crew surviving.
*   A Jetways Airlines Fokker 50 crashed during a humanitarian aid flight from Mogadishu to Ceel Barde, Somalia. The aircraft ran off the runway upon arrival at its destination, striking a house and resulting in the loss of one of the four occupants.
*   A Northwestern Air British Aerospace Jetstream crashed shortly after takeoff while transporting mine workers from Fort Smith, Northwest Territories, to the Diavik Diamond Mine in the Northwest Territories, Canada. Tragically, six of the seven passengers and crew lost their lives as the aircraft made impact with the ground 500 meters (1600 feet) from the end of the runway.

**February 2024:**

*   Air Serbia Flight 324, operated by Marathon Airlines using an Embraer 195, hit the landing lights during takeoff at Belgrade Nikola Tesla Airport. The aircraft continued to fly for another hour before making an emergency landing back at the same airport, despite sustaining a large hole in its fuselage. Remarkably, all 111 occupants on board survived without injury.

### **March 2024:**

*   In the 2024 Nairobi mid-air collision, Safarilink Aviation Flight 53, a De Havilland Canada Dash 8, collided with a Cessna 172. The collision resulted in the Cessna 172 crashing and killing both of its occupants, while the Dash 8 managed to land safely.
*   LATAM Airlines Flight 800, a Boeing 787-9 traveling from Sydney to Auckland, experienced an in-flight upset that resulted in injuries to 50 passengers. Despite the incident, the flight landed safely at Auckland Airport.
*   In the 2024 Malakal Airport collision, a Safe Air Company Boeing 727-200 on a cargo flight from Juba Airport undershot the runway and collided with an MD-82 while attempting to land at Malakal Airport, South Sudan. All seven crew members on board survived, with one sustaining injuries.

### **May 2024:**

*   During Singapore Airlines Flight 321 from London-Heathrow to Singapore, carrying 229 people, the Boeing 777-300ER encountered severe turbulence, [resulting in one passenger’s death and injuring 30 others](https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2024/05/21/singapore-airlines-london-sq321/). The plane made an emergency landing in Bangkok.

### **July 2024:**

*   Gazpromavia Flight 9608, a Sukhoi Superjet 100, was on a ferry flight from Lukhovitsy to Moscow when it crashed during an emergency landing attempt near Moscow. Tragically, all three crew members lost their lives in the accident.
*   A Saurya Airlines Bombardier CRJ-200ER crashed shortly after departing from Kathmandu Tribhuvan Airport on its way to Pokhara International Airport, resulting in the deaths of 18 of the 19 people on board.

### **August 2024:**

*   Voepass Flight 2283, an ATR-72-500 flying from Cascavel Airport to Guarulhos International Airport in São Paulo, Brazil, entered a flat spin and crashed in Vinhedo, São Paulo, killing all 62 people on board.
*   Thai Flying Service Flight 209, a Cessna 208 Grand Caravan traveling from Bangkok to Ko Mai Si, Thailand, crashed in a mangrove swamp shortly after takeoff from Suvarnabhumi Airport, killing all nine occupants.
*   A Vityaz-Aero Mil Mi-8T helicopter crashed near the Vachkazhets volcano in Kamchatka Krai, Russia, during poor weather conditions, killing all 22 people on board.

### **November 2024:**

*   Total Linhas Aéreas Flight 5682, a Boeing 737-4Q8 (SF), experienced an in-flight fire in the cargo hold while en route from Vitória to Guarulhos, Brazil. The aircraft made an emergency landing in Guarulhos; both crew members survived, but the plane was destroyed by fire.
*   Swiftair Flight 5960, a Boeing 737-400SF operating on behalf of DHL, crashed near a two-story house during its approach to Vilnius, Lithuania, killing one of the four crew members.
*   Swiss International Air Lines Flight 1885, an Airbus A220-300 flying from Bucharest to Zurich, made an emergency landing at Graz Airport after an engine failure caused smoke in the cabin. The aircraft was evacuated using emergency slides; 17 passengers and five crew members were hospitalized, and one flight attendant later died from injuries.

### **December 2024:**

*   Azerbaijan Airlines Flight 8243, an Embraer 190AR, crashed near Aktau, Kazakhstan, during an emergency landing after being damaged by a Russian surface-to-air missile detonation. Of the 67 people on board, 38 were killed.
*   Jeju Air Flight 2216, a Boeing 737-800, struck an embankment and exploded while attempting to land at Muan International Airport in South Korea. Of the 181 people on board, 179 were killed. The crash remains the deadliest accident involving a Boeing 737 Next Generation and the deadliest aviation disaster in South Korea.

## 2023 Commercial Airplane Crashes:

In 2023, commercial aviation achieved unprecedented safety levels, surpassing all previous years. As noted by a prominent air safety expert, the year marked a historic milestone with the lowest number of accidents and fatalities recorded.

### **January 2023:**

*   Yeti Airlines Flight 691: an ATR 72-500 aircraft operating a domestic flight from Tribhuvan International Airport to Pokhara International Airport in Nepal crashed into the gorge of the Seti Gandaki River, resulting in the loss of all 72 individuals on board.

### **February 2023:**

*   Coulson Aviation crash: a Boeing 737-300 aircraft owned by Coulson Aviation and serving as an air tanker, experienced a crash at Fitzgerald River National Park in the Great Southern Region of Western Australia while the aircraft was engaged in firefighting operations to combat multiple fires. Fortunately, both occupants on board managed to survive the crash, only sustaining minor injuries.

### **June 2023:**

*   A SAM Air Cessna Grand Caravan crashed on a domestic flight in Papua, Indonesia, resulting in the fatalities of all 4 passengers and 2 crew members.

### **July 2023:**

*   A Halla Airlines Embraer EMB 120 Brasilia crashed during landing at Aden Adde International Airport in Mogadishu, Somalia. Fortunately, all 34 occupants survived the incident, with 2 passengers sustaining minor injuries.

### **September 2023:**

*   Ural Airlines Flight 1383, an Airbus A320 flying from Sochi to Omsk in Russia, executed an emergency landing in a cornfield due to hydraulic issues. Miraculously, all 165 passengers and crew on board escaped unharmed.
*   A Manaus Aerotaxi Embraer Bandeirante crashed into an embankment while performing a go-around approach to Barcelos Airport in Brazil, resulting in the tragic loss of all 14 occupants.

### **October 2023:**

*   Alaska Airlines Flight 2059, operated by Horizon Air, diverted to Portland after an off-duty pilot attempted to shut off both engines mid-flight. The pilot was apprehended upon landing, and there were no injuries reported.
*   The 2023 Rio Branco Cessna Grand Caravan crash involved a Cessna 208B Caravan operated by ART Táxi Aéreo, which tragically crashed and exploded shortly after takeoff from Rio Branco International Airport in Brazil, claiming the lives of all 12 individuals on board.

## 2022 Commercial Airplane Crashes:

**March 2022:**

*   A China Eastern Airlines Boeing 737-800 plane crashed in the mountains of Guangxi near Guangzhou, China, leading to the tragic loss of all 133 people on board.

### **April 2022:**

*   A DHL Aviation Boeing 757-200 freighter crashed near the runway at Juan Santamaria Airport in San Juan, Costa Rica. All crew members managed to escape with minor injuries.

### **May 2022:**

*   The crash of a Tibet Airlines Airbus A319 at Chongqing Jiangbei International Airport while taking off. The plane caught on fire, but luckily, all the people on board survived.
*   A Tara Air DHC-6 Twin Otter crashes in the Mustang region of Nepal. Unfortunately, all 22 people on board were killed.

### **June 2022:**

*   A Red Air McDonnell Douglas MD-82 crash-lands and catches on fire while landing at Miami International Airport. All the people on board survived, with 3 occupants being hospitalized for minor injuries.

### **July 2022:**

*   The tragic crash of Meridian Flight 3032 occurred near Kavala, Greece, resulting in the loss of all eight individuals on board. The aircraft, an Antonov An-12, was carrying a cargo of weapons and ammunition from Niš, Serbia, destined for Dhaka, Bangladesh.
*   Jubba Airways Crash 2022: A Fokker 50 aircraft operated by the airline crashed and overturned upon landing in Mogadishu, Somalia. Out of the 36 individuals on board, 16 sustained injuries.

### **September 2022:**

*   Tragically, in the Mutiny Bay plane crash of 2022, a DHC-3 Turbine Otter aircraft transporting tourists from Friday Harbor Seaplane Base in Washington to Renton Municipal Airport experienced a sudden nosedive into the sea. Regrettably, all ten individuals on board lost their lives in the incident.

### **October 2022:**

*   Korean Air Flight 631, an Airbus A330-300 aircraft departing from Seoul-Incheon International Airport, experienced an unfortunate incident when the plane overshot the runway during its third landing attempt at Mactan-Cebu International Airport in the Philippines. The adverse weather conditions were identified as the contributing factor. Thankfully, none of the 173 passengers and crew members sustained any injuries. But the aircraft itself suffered irreparable damage.

### **November 2022:**

*   Precision Air Flight 494, an ATR 42-500 aircraft operating a domestic flight from Dar es Salaam, crashed into Lake Victoria while attempting to land at Bukoba Airport in Tanzania. Out of the 43 individuals on board, 19 lost their lives in the accident.
*   LATAM Perú Flight 2213, an Airbus A320neo-271N operated by LATAM Chile, encountered a collision during takeoff from Lima to Juliaca. The aircraft collided with a fire engine that was crossing the runway, resulting in the unfortunate deaths of two firefighters and injury to a third individual. All passengers and crew remained unharmed.

# U.S. Air Carrier Safety Data

**Embedded Dataset Excel:**

**Dataset Excel:**

[table_02_09_072726.xlsx](https://www.bts.gov/sites/bts.dot.gov/files/2026-07/table_02_09_072726.xlsx) (31.67 KB)

**Notes:**

_Aircraft-miles_, _Aircraft departures_, and _Flight hours_ are compiled by the U.S. Department of Transportation, Federal Aviation Administration. Rates are computed by dividing the number of _Fatalities_, _Seriously injured persons_, _Total accidents_, and _Fatal accidents_ by the number of _Aircraft-miles_, _Aircraft departures_, or _Flight hours_. These figures are based on information provided by airlines to the U.S. Department of Transportation, Bureau of Transportation Statistics, Office of Airline Information. The illegal acts, such as suicide, sabotage and terrorism, are included in the totals for accidents, fatalities, and rate computation. 1991 data do not include the 12 persons killed aboard a SkyWest commuter aircraft when it and a U.S. Air aircraft collided. For 2001, fatalities resulting from the September 11 terrorist acts are excluded, other than the persons aboard the aircraft who were killed.

**Description:**

**KEY:** N = data do not exist; R = revised; U = data are not available.

a Air carriers operating under 14 CFR 121, scheduled and nonscheduled service. Includes all scheduled and nonscheduled service accidents involving all-cargo carriers and commercial operators of large aircraft when those accidents occurred during 14 CFR 121 operations. Since Mar. 20, 1997, 14 CFR 121 includes aircraft with 10 or more seats formerly operated under 14 CFR 135. This change makes it difficult to compare pre-1997 data for 14 CFR 121 and 14 CFR 135 with more recent data.

**Source:**

**Fatalities, accidents, miles, departures, and flight hours:**

1960: National Transportation Safety Board,_Annual Review of Aircraft Accident Data: U.S. Air Carrier Operations_, Calendar Year 1967 (Washington, DC: December 1968).

1965-70: National Transportation Safety Board,Calendar Year 1975, NTSB/ARC-77/1 (Washington, DC: January 1977).

1975 (all categories except miles): National Transportation Safety Board,Calendar Year 1983, NTSB/ARC-87/01 (Washington, DC: February 1987), table 18.

1975 (miles): National Transportation Safety Board,Calendar Year 1975, NTSB/ARC-77/1 (Washington, DC: January 1977 ).

1980: National Transportation Safety Board,Calendar Year 1981, NTSB/ARC-85/01 (Washington, DC: February 1985), tables 2 and 16.

1985-2024: National Transportation Safety Board,_Aviation Accident Statistics_, table 5, available at [https://www.ntsb.gov/safety/Pages/research.aspx](https://www.ntsb.gov/safety/Pages/research.aspx) as of Feb. 10, 2026.

**Serious injuries:**

1970-85: National Transportation Safety Board,_Annual Review of Aircraft Accident Data: U.S. Air Carrier Operations_(Washington, DC: Annual Issues).

1990-2024: National Transportation Safety Board,Analysis and Data Division, personal communication, May 20, 2024, Feb. 4, 2025, Jul. 8, 2026.

**Notes:**

_Aircraft-miles_, _Aircraft departures_, and _Flight hours_ are compiled by the U.S. Department of Transportation, Federal Aviation Administration. Rates are computed by dividing the number of _Fatalities_, _Seriously injured persons_, _Total accidents_, and _Fatal accidents_ by the number of _Aircraft-miles_, _Aircraft departures_, or _Flight hours_. These figures are based on information provided by airlines to the U.S. Department of Transportation, Bureau of Transportation Statistics, Office of Airline Information. The illegal acts, such as suicide, sabotage and terrorism, are included in the totals for accidents, fatalities, and rate computation. 1991 data do not include the 12 persons killed aboard a SkyWest commuter aircraft when it and a U.S. Air aircraft collided. For 2001, fatalities resulting from the September 11 terrorist acts are excluded, other than the persons aboard the aircraft who were killed.

# Safety Topics

## Airplane Crashes

Commercial scheduled air travel is among the safest modes of[**transportation**](https://injuryfacts.nsc.org/home-and-community/safety-topics/deaths-by-transportation-mode/); the lifetime odds of dying as an aircraft passenger in the United States was too small to calculate. Preliminary estimates of the total number of accidents involving a U.S. registered civilian aircraft decreased from 1,216 in 2023 to 1,201 in 2024. The number of civil aviation deaths decreased from 327 in 2023 to 321 in 2024. All but 5 of the 321 deaths in 2024 were onboard fatalities. None of these deaths involved a commercial scheduled airline.

Use the interactive chart to explore aviation accident trends by U.S. air carrier category. Major airlines (scheduled service) experienced no onboard fatalities and had a fatal accident rate of 0.0 per 100,000 flight hours in 2024. This contrasts sharply with general aviation, which experienced 300 onboard fatalities and had a fatal accident rate of 0.721 per 100,000 flight hours.

The F-35 crash on May 28, 2024 was one of the most significant events of the year. Here is a video we put together about the response and news coverage of the event. This plane crash resulted in a large, multi-agency response and national news coverage. Bernalillo County Fire, Albuquerque Fire and Kirtland AFB FD all responded. The pilot suffered serious injuries and was transported by Rescue 1 to the hospital. No other injuries were reported but responders were monitored following the crash due to the nature of the aircraft. This concludes the look back at significant events of 2024. It was another very busy year for AFR. Thank you all for following along and thank you for the continued support. #albuquerque #abqfirerescue

# Federal investigators probe Amazon cargo jet's fiery runway crash that killed 5 in Miami

5 killed were all inside a van

![Image 3: NTSB chair calls Miami Amazon cargo plane crash scene 'devastating'](https://cdn.abcotvs.com/dip/images/19803640_090726-wls-ntsb-miami-crash-n1-4p-vid.jpg)

NTSB chair calls Amazon cargo plane crash scene 'devastating' and says flight and voice recorders have been recovered.

By DAVID FISCHER, MARC LEVY and JEFFREY COLLINS![Image 4: AP logo](https://cdn.abcotvs.net/abcotv/static/common/origins/origin-ap.png)

Monday, September 7, 2026

Share

MIAMI -- The [five people killed](https://abc7ny.com/story/amazon-cargo-plane-sends-billowing-cloud-smoke-overrunning-runway-miami-airport/19799551/)when an Amazon cargo jet ran off a runway at Miami International Airport were all inside a van carrying seven people from a cleaning company, and an SUV hit outside of airport property, National Transportation Safety Board Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said Monday.

Homendy called the scene of Sunday’s crash “utter devastation.” She didn’t detail how many people were in the SUV or where the dead were located.

![Image 5: An Amazon cargo plane sits at the Miami International Airport (MIA) after it overshot the runway, Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026. ](https://cdn.abcotvs.com/dip/images/19801839_090726-cc-ap-amazon-plane-crash-img.jpg)

An Amazon cargo plane sits at the Miami International Airport (MIA) after it overshot the runway, Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026.

AP Photo/Lynne Sladky

Homendy walked the route the Boeing 767 followed, noting tire marks from the pavement into the grass, the destroyed van carrying the cleaning crew, torn fencing, navigational equipment, and the crushed SUV outside airport property.

The debris included vehicle air bags, equipment from the vehicles, the airplane and the airport, and “fencing everywhere,” Homendy said.

“It’s pretty extensive. Hard to see and I’m sure it must have been very difficult for the responders as well,” Homendy said.

The airline, all told, traveled about 1,300 feet (396 meters) past the paved surface. Debris was everywhere, she said.

“I would describe it in one word as devastating, utter devastation,” Homendy said.

The van with seven people inside was “torn apart. It certainly must have been devastating,” she said. The van was owned by Professional Ocean Service Corp., an airline cleaning contractor.

Homendy said the NTSB would issue more information on Tuesday, including possibly information on speed that is confirmed by the flight data recorder.

Federal investigators examining the crash spent Monday determining whether the plane touched down too late to stop safely.

Video of Sunday’s landing appears to show the Boeing 767 remaining airborne well down the runway before touching down. Aviation experts said investigators will seek to determine exactly where the plane landed, whether it was beyond the normal touchdown zone, and why the pilots did not abandon the landing.

Investigators will also examine the plane’s speed and braking, weather and wind conditions, the aircraft’s mechanical condition and other factors that could have contributed to the deadly overrun.

The aircraft on Sunday flew from Cincinnati to Miami and then to San Juan, Puerto Rico. It was returning to Miami when it overran the runway around 2 p.m. and plowed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport.

Aside from the five who died, three people were critically injured and two others were hospitalized with less severe injuries, officials said.

The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.

## Top Stories

[![Image 6](https://cdn.abcotvs.com/dip/images/19843748_091726-wabc-crane-collapse-img.jpg) ## Crane collapse damages at least two homes in River Vale * 21 minutes ago](https://abc7ny.com/post/river-vale-crane-collapse-damages-least-homes-nj/19843729/)

[![Image 8](https://cdn.abcotvs.com/dip/images/19841197_091626-wabc-shlonsky-bay-ridge-murder-folo-redo-6pm.jpg) ## Husband admits to killing pre-K teacher wife with tool during argument, police say * 2 hours ago](https://abc7ny.com/post/husband-admits-killing-pre-teacher-wife-tool-during-argument-brooklyn-police-say/19843573/)

The typical landing zone for a plane is within the first 3,000 feet (914 meters) of a runway, experts said. If the cargo jet was beyond that area, it should have aborted the landing and gone around for another try, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said.

Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former Inspector General of the Transportation Department, said video posted online shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.

It wasn’t raining at the time, but dark storm clouds loomed and strong winds were reported. Schiavo said that if the plane had a tail wind, that could have contributed to it floating further down the runway.

“A tail wind would certainly add to your troubles if you’ve already given up a good chunk of the runway by not touching down and landing right away,” Schiavo said.

The Miami airport is not equipped with arresting systems that the FAA says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide to safely stop planes that do go past the end of a runway. Those beds of lightweight, crushable material at the end of a runway have been credited by the FAA with helping save at least 497 lives aboard planes that overran runways.

Miami’s airport appears to be in compliance and wasn’t required to have an arresting system because it has a 1,000-foot safety buffer at the end of its runways, said Mike O’Donnell, the FAA’s former director of airport safety and accident investigations.

The requirement was prompted by American Airlines Flight 1420[overrunning a runway](https://apnews.com/domestic-news-general-news-dc6946924ccf4b449e091682845378b0)at Little Rock National Airport in Arkansas in 1999, killing nine.

The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semitrucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.

The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.

Schiavo said the NTSB will also closely examine the maintenance history of this plane — particularly since it has a history of foreign ownership, including by a Russian company.

The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of Sunday afternoon and continued to hamper air travel into Monday.

Miami International Airport said that two of its four runways remained closed Monday and that operations were to be affected throughout the day because of aircraft and flight crews not arriving there due to Sunday’s cancellations after the crash.

An airport spokesperson said there were 160 cancellations and more than 300 delayed flights Sunday, plus another 69 canceled flights Monday through mid-afternoon. Flight tracking sites were reporting widespread delays at the airport.

Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.

“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport," the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”

Last year, a[UPS plane crashed](https://apnews.com/article/ups-cargo-plane-explosion-louisville-deaths-af12da7f8611bad0bf0cb664de189250)after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport. The crash killed all[three pilots](https://apnews.com/article/ups-plane-crash-explosion-kentucky-pilots-victims-8b133072a1144e4c547c6468df0854ab)and[12 people](https://apnews.com/article/ups-plane-crash-louisville-deaths-aac761ad3155ca73f9d490b74e0fde43)on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured.

_Levy reported from Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, and Collins reported from Columbia, South Carolina. Associated Press writer Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, contributed._

The van with seven people inside was “torn apart. It certainly must have been devastating,” she said. The van was owned by Professional Ocean Service Corp., an airline cleaning contractor.

Homendy said the NTSB would issue more information on Tuesday, including possibly information on speed that is confirmed by the flight data recorder.

Federal investigators examining the crash spent Monday determining whether the plane touched down too late to stop safely.

Video of Sunday’s landing appears to show the Boeing 767 remaining airborne well down the runway before touching down. Aviation experts said investigators will seek to determine exactly where the plane landed, whether it was beyond the normal touchdown zone, and why the pilots did not abandon the landing.

Investigators will also examine the plane’s speed and braking, weather and wind conditions, the aircraft’s mechanical condition and other factors that could have contributed to the deadly overrun.

The aircraft on Sunday flew from Cincinnati to Miami and then to San Juan, Puerto Rico. It was returning to Miami when it overran the runway around 2 p.m. and plowed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport.

Aside from the five who died, three people were critically injured and two others were hospitalized with less severe injuries, officials said.

The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.

The typical landing zone for a plane is within the first 3,000 feet (914 meters) of a runway, experts said. If the cargo jet was beyond that area, it should have aborted the landing and gone around for another try, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said.

Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former Inspector General of the Transportation Department, said video posted online shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.

It wasn’t raining at the time, but dark storm clouds loomed and strong winds were reported. Schiavo said that if the plane had a tail wind, that could have contributed to it floating further down the runway.

“A tail wind would certainly add to your troubles if you’ve already given up a good chunk of the runway by not touching down and landing right away,” Schiavo said.

The Miami airport is not equipped with arresting systems that the FAA says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide to safely stop planes that do go past the end of a runway. Those beds of lightweight, crushable material at the end of a runway have been credited by the FAA with helping save at least 497 lives aboard planes that overran runways.

Miami’s airport appears to be in compliance and wasn’t required to have an arresting system because it has a 1,000-foot safety buffer at the end of its runways, said Mike O’Donnell, the FAA’s former director of airport safety and accident investigations.

The requirement was prompted by American Airlines Flight 1420[overrunning a runway](https://apnews.com/domestic-news-general-news-dc6946924ccf4b449e091682845378b0)at Little Rock National Airport in Arkansas in 1999, killing nine.

The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semitrucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.

The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.

Schiavo said the NTSB will also closely examine the maintenance history of this plane — particularly since it has a history of foreign ownership, including by a Russian company.

The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of Sunday afternoon and continued to hamper air travel into Monday.

Miami International Airport said that two of its four runways remained closed Monday and that operations were to be affected throughout the day because of aircraft and flight crews not arriving there due to Sunday’s cancellations after the crash.

An airport spokesperson said there were 160 cancellations and more than 300 delayed flights Sunday, plus another 69 canceled flights Monday through mid-afternoon. Flight tracking sites were reporting widespread delays at the airport.

Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.

“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport," the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”

On January 29, 2025, a [Bombardier CRJ700](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombardier_CRJ700_series "Bombardier CRJ700 series") airliner operating as **American Airlines Flight 5342** (operated by [PSA Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PSA_Airlines "PSA Airlines") as [American Eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Eagle_(airline_brand) "American Eagle (airline brand)"))[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-Eagle-4) and a United States Army [Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikorsky_UH-60_Black_Hawk "Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk") helicopter operating as **Priority Air Transport 25**[collided in mid-air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-air_collision "Mid-air collision") over the [Potomac River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potomac_River "Potomac River") in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") The collision occurred at 8:47 p.m. at an altitude of about 300 feet (100 m) and about one-half mile (800 m) short of the threshold of runway 33 at [Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan_Washington_National_Airport "Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport") in [Arlington, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_County,_Virginia "Arlington County, Virginia"). All 67 people aboard both aircraft were killed in the crash, 64 passengers and crew on the airliner and the three crew of the helicopter. It was the first major US commercial passenger flight crash since [Colgan Air Flight 3407](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colgan_Air_Flight_3407 "Colgan Air Flight 3407") in 2009, and the deadliest US air disaster since the crash of [American Airlines Flight 587](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Airlines_Flight_587 "American Airlines Flight 587") in 2001.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-11)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-AP_News_2025-12) This was also the third [hull loss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hull_loss "Hull loss") and first fatal accident involving the CRJ700 series.

The jet was on [final approach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_approach "Final approach") into Reagan National Airport after flying a scheduled route from [Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita_Dwight_D._Eisenhower_National_Airport "Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport") in [Wichita, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita,_Kansas "Wichita, Kansas"), to D.C., while the helicopter crew was performing a required annual flying evaluation with [night vision goggles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_vision_goggles "Night vision goggles") and had left from [Davison Army Airfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davison_Army_Airfield "Davison Army Airfield") in [Fairfax County, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax_County,_Virginia "Fairfax County, Virginia"). Both aircraft communicated with [air traffic control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_traffic_control "Air traffic control") before they collided. The helicopter crew reported twice that they had visual contact with the airliner and would maintain separation from it, although it is unknown whether they were monitoring the correct aircraft. The crew of the Black Hawk may not have heard parts of the tower communication due to a mic press.

On March 11, the [National Transportation Safety Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Transportation_Safety_Board "National Transportation Safety Board") (NTSB) released a preliminary report along with urgent safety recommendations, highlighting the dangerously narrow vertical separation between the runway approach path and the helicopter route. The NTSB chair also expressed anger that the [Federal Aviation Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Aviation_Administration "Federal Aviation Administration") (FAA) did not act on data showing the number of near-miss alerts over the previous decade.

The final report, released on February 17, 2026, concluded that the [probable causes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probable_cause "Probable cause") of the crash included the FAA's placement of the helicopter route, failures in the agency's oversight, and an overreliance on [visual separation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_meteorological_conditions "Visual meteorological conditions"). Also causal was helicopter [pilot error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilot_error "Pilot error"), loss of [situational awareness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Situation_awareness "Situation awareness") by air traffic control due to high workload, and the [United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army")'s failure to ensure pilot understanding of [altimeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altimeter "Altimeter") error tolerances.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-13)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-AIR-26-02_Final_Report-7)

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

### Aircraft

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Aircraft")]

Flight 5342 was operated by a 20-year-old [Bombardier CRJ700](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombardier_CRJ700_series "Bombardier CRJ700 series"), a regional jet commonly used for short- to medium-haul flights. It was configured as a CRJ701ER, denoting extended range. Manufactured in September 2004, it bore the manufacturer's [serial number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serial_number "Serial number") 10165 and was [registered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_registration "Aircraft registration") as N709PS.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-14)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-15) PSA Airlines is owned by the [American Airlines Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Airlines_Group "American Airlines Group"),[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-16) which is also the parent company of American Airlines.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-CBS:_What_we_know-17) No problems were reported as the plane took off from Wichita on its way to Washington.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-Harvey-2025-6)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-Regan-2025-5) Flight 5342's route had been operated for about one year;[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-Draper-18) previously, [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas "Kansas") residents had needed to drive to adjacent [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri") and [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma") if they wanted to take direct flights to the East Coast.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-Draper-18) A year earlier, local leaders had finally convinced American Airlines to establish direct passenger air service from Kansas to the [East Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Coast_of_the_United_States "East Coast of the United States").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-Draper-18)

The helicopter involved was a [US Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army") Sikorsky UH-60L Black Hawk[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-19) with the [serial number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_military_aircraft_serial_numbers "United States military aircraft serial numbers")00-26860.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-Aerotime-8) The helicopter was configured for use as executive transportation for senior US officials and soldiers, and was flying under the callsign PAT25 indicating a "Priority Air Transport" flight.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-Regan-2025-5)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-AAFC_1-20) No senior officials were on board the helicopter.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-Regan-2025-5)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-AAFC_1-20) The helicopter, of B Company of the [12th Aviation Battalion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/12th_Aviation_Battalion_(United_States) "12th Aviation Battalion (United States)") at [Fort Belvoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Belvoir "Fort Belvoir"), was on an annual and [night vision goggles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night-vision_device "Night-vision device") check flight out of [Davison Army Airfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davison_Army_Airfield "Davison Army Airfield") when the collision occurred.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-Davison-9)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-NTSB2025-02-14-21)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-CNN-Jan29-Quote-22) The helicopter was part of the [Continuity of Government Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuity_of_Government_Plan "Continuity of Government Plan"), with the flight being a routine evaluation of aircrew in night flight along the corridor. In emergencies, elements of the US government would use it to evacuate the capital.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-23)

### Passengers and crew

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Passengers and crew")]

See also: § Casualties

The airliner carried 60 passengers and four crew members: a [captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilot_in_command "Pilot in command"), a [first officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_officer_(aviation) "First officer (aviation)") and two [flight attendants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_attendant "Flight attendant"):[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-NTSB_Preliminary_Report-10):1,3

*   Captain Jonathan Campos, 34, was the pilot flying and had been with the airline for six years. He had logged 3,950 flight hours, including 3,024 on CRJ-series aircraft, and was a [Federal Flight Deck Officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Flight_Deck_Officer "Federal Flight Deck Officer").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-NTSB_Preliminary_Report-10):3[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-24)
*   First Officer Samuel Lilley, 28, was the pilot monitoring. He had worked for the airline for two years and accumulated 2,469 flight hours, with 966 on the CRJ.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-NTSB_Preliminary_Report-10):3

The helicopter had a crew of three Army personnel:

*   [Captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(United_States_O-3) "Captain (United States O-3)") Rebecca Lobach, 28, was the [pilot flying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilot_flying "Pilot flying") and undergoing her annual night flying evaluation. She had accumulated 450 [flight hours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_time "Flight time") at the time of the crash, with 326 on UH-60 type helicopters.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-VPM_2025-25)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-26)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-27)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-NTSB_Preliminary_Report-10):3
*   [Chief Warrant Officer 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Warrant_Officer_2 "Chief Warrant Officer 2") Andrew Eaves, 39, was the [evaluator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Check_pilot "Check pilot") for Lobach and was serving as the [pilot monitoring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilot_monitoring "Pilot monitoring") who primarily communicated with air traffic controllers. He had 968 flight hours, with 886 on the UH-60.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-TimesSchmitt-28)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-29)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-30)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-NTSB_Preliminary_Report-10):3
*   [Staff Sergeant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staff_sergeant_(U.S._Army) "Staff sergeant (U.S. Army)") Ryan O'Hara, 29, was the crew chief ([aircraft maintenance technician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_maintenance_technician "Aircraft maintenance technician")), with 1,149 flight hours, all being on the UH-60.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-31)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-CBS:_What_we_know-17)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-NTSB_Preliminary_Report-10):3

### Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport")]

The airspace around Reagan National Airport is among the world's most complex and closely monitored, with [restrictions on both sides of the Potomac River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C.,_Special_Flight_Rules_Area "Washington, D.C., Special Flight Rules Area") to protect government buildings in Washington, D.C.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-32) Efforts have been made to reduce congestion, but in 2024, Congress approved additional flights.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-33) Military helicopter operations further complicated the airspace, including a helicopter corridor which passes within 15 feet (4.6 m) vertically of the approach to runway 33.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-34)

Reagan National has three runways: 1/19, 15/33, and 4/22. Runways 1/19 handle 95% of commercial aircraft arrivals. Runway 33 handles about 4%, and runway 15—due to its close proximity to the [Pentagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pentagon "The Pentagon")[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]—handles fewer than 1%.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-NTSB_Preliminary_Report-10):18 Runways 4/22 are rarely used for commercial aircraft, mainly smaller aircraft on short routes to the Northeast.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-35) During north operations, which were in effect at the time of the collision, most arrivals occur on runway 1, with intermittent arrivals on runway 33, depending on traffic demands and separation requirements.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-NTSB_Preliminary_Report-10):10 The use of runway 33 is typically limited to smaller aircraft,[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] which are able to land on its relatively short 5,204-foot-long (1,586 m) surface.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-NTSB_Preliminary_Report-10):12

_[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ reported that as of September 2023, the tower at Reagan Airport was nearly a third below targeted staffing levels. The staffing shortage has forced many controllers to work up to six days a week and 10 hours daily.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-Ember_2025-36)

On the night of the collision, air traffic control (ATC) staffing was below the typical level for that time and traffic volume, according to a preliminary Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) safety report.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-Ember_2025-36) Normally, the tower had six[_[dubious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Accuracy\_dispute#Disputed\_statement "Wikipedia:Accuracy dispute")–[discuss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk:2025\_Potomac\_River\_mid-air\_collision#Dubious "Talk:2025 Potomac River mid-air collision")_] controllers: assistant local control, ground control, clearance delivery, local control, and an operations supervisor.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-NTSB_Preliminary_Report-10):10

At 9:30 p.m., when air traffic usually decreases, the helicopter control and local control positions are typically combined.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] However, on the day of the collision, the supervisor merged those positions at 3:40 p.m.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-NTSB_Preliminary_Report-10):10 allowing one controller to leave early. The air traffic controllers' union cautioned against assuming that the combined role would make conditions unsafe.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-37)

Helicopter control and local control operate on different radio frequencies, meaning the crews of Flight 5342 and PAT25 were not able to hear each other's transmissions to the controller, but both could hear the controller's responses.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-NTSB_Preliminary_Report-10):10

## Accident

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Accident")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Preliminary_map_for_2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision.jpg/250px-Preliminary_map_for_2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Preliminary_map_for_2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision.jpg)

Map of the flight paths of the helicopter and regional jet, with an approximate location of the collision

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/N709PS_PAT25_Flight_Paths.png/250px-N709PS_PAT25_Flight_Paths.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:N709PS_PAT25_Flight_Paths.png)

NTSB graphic of the flight paths

At 8:43 p.m. [EST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Standard_Time "Eastern Standard Time") (2025-01-30T01:43[UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC "UTC")), as American Airlines Flight 5342 was flying a visual approach to runway 1, it made initial contact with the Reagan National control tower. The controller asked if the crew could switch to runway 33. The crew accepted the request and were subsequently cleared to land on runway 33. The helicopter was about 1.1 [nautical miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nautical_mile "Nautical mile") (2.0 km; 1.3 mi) west of the [Key Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_Bridge_(Washington,_D.C.) "Key Bridge (Washington, D.C.)") following Helicopter Route 1 to Helicopter Route 4. At 8:46 p.m., around two minutes before the collision, the controller called the helicopter crew, advising them of a CRJ700, at an altitude of 1,200 feet (370 m) south of the [Woodrow Wilson Memorial Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson_Memorial_Bridge "Woodrow Wilson Memorial Bridge"), circling runway 33. The part of the transmission advising that the CRJ was "circling" was not captured by the helicopter's [cockpit voice recorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cockpit_voice_recorder "Cockpit voice recorder") (CVR) and may not have been heard by the helicopter crew. The helicopter crew acknowledged that they had the jet in sight and requested [visual separation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_flight_rules "Visual flight rules")—meaning that they could see and maintain separation from the aircraft on their own—which the controller approved. However, it remains unclear if they had acknowledged the correct aircraft.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-NTSB2025-02-14-21)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-Peluffo_2025-38)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-39)

At 8:47 p.m. EST, 20 seconds before the collision, the controller asked the helicopter crew if they had the CRJ in sight. An audible air traffic radar conflict alert in the background of the transmission was present. One second later, the airliner crew received an automatic [traffic advisory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_collision_avoidance_system#Types_of_traffic_and_resolution_advisories "Traffic collision avoidance system") from their [traffic collision avoidance system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_collision_avoidance_system "Traffic collision avoidance system") (TCAS) which was accompanied by an [audible announcement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice_warning_system "Voice warning system") in the cockpit, "traffic; traffic." However, TCAS [resolution advisories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_collision_avoidance_system#Types_of_traffic_and_resolution_advisories "Traffic collision avoidance system") with audible instructions like "climb; climb" or "descend; descend" are automatically disabled when an aircraft is below 900 feet (270 m) above ground level to avoid guiding an aircraft into potential collisions with terrain or other aircraft in congested terminal airspace.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-Regan-2025-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-NTSB_Preliminary_Report-10):9 TCAS traffic advisories are disabled below 400 feet (120 m).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-NTSB_Preliminary_Report-10):9

Seventeen seconds before the collision, the controller instructed the helicopter to pass behind Flight 5342.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] One of the helicopter crew members depressed a mic for 0.8 seconds to communicate with the controller during this transmission, which may have caused the "pass behind" part of the transmission to be missed by the helicopter crew.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The helicopter crew again confirmed they had an airplane in sight and requested visual separation from the airliner, which the controller approved again.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Fifteen seconds before the crash, flight instructor and co-pilot Chief Warrant Officer 2 Andrew Loyd Eaves asked the pilot, Capt. Rebecca M. Lobach, to change course by making a sharp left to the east river bank. Capt. Lobach acknowledged the request and attempted to execute it, but failed.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-40) Seven seconds before the collision, the airliner "rolled out on final" (finished its turn) to line up with runway 33. One second before the crash, the airliner increased its pitch with its [elevators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator_(aeronautics) "Elevator (aeronautics)") deflected close to their maximum nose-up travel.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Potomac_River_mid-air_collision#cite_note-NTSB2025-02-14-21)
