The statistics cover the full budget years 2020-2023 and then the first 10 months of the 2024 budget year, through July 31. In those 10 months of last year, 25 service members and Defense Department civilian employees were killed and 14 aircraft were destroyed.

“These accident rates are incredibly troubling and demand action," Warren told the AP in an emailed statement. She said legislative changes to make accident reports more accessible "are desperately needed so Congress can understand the root causes of these accidents to save service member lives.”

## Several military aircraft have been especially prone to crashing

The Osprey, which flies like a plane but converts to land like a helicopter, has been among the most dangerous aircraft, as the AP has reported extensively.

In addition, the new Defense Department data shows the Apache helicopter had about 4.5 times the rate of the most serious Class A accidents during the 2024 budget year compared with four years earlier. The C-130 transport plane, a workhorse of the military, nearly doubled its rate over the same period, even as it reported safer years in between.

[![Image 31: National Guard aircraft crashes in Oklahoma; no injuries reported](https://kubrick.htvapps.com/htv-prod-media.s3.amazonaws.com/images/poster-image-2025-10-23t152523-977-68fa8f4e048a4.jpg?crop=1.00xw%3A1.00xh%3B0%2C0&resize=136%3A*) National Guard aircraft crashes during training mission in Oklahoma; no injuries reported](https://www.kcra.com/article/national-guard-aircraft-crash-oklahoma-city/69144096)

The Pentagon, when asked about these trends, did not immediately respond.

The Navy's data on just its own aviation mishaps shows a marked increase this year. The Naval Safety Command reported eight Class A aviation mishaps in 2024. In 2025, that total has spiked to 14.

Aviation expert and former military pilot John Nance said the ever-growing demands being placed on military pilots are most likely playing a major part in the growing number of mishaps.

“Whether we’re talking about the end of Afghanistan, whether we talk about deployments to Djibouti, or the back and forth across Saudi Arabia to get to the Emirates, I think that as the pace (of military operations) ticks up, the mishaps are going to tick up,” Nance said.

## This year has seen a series of accidents

While the data does not continue into 2025, there have been multiple high-profile aviation mishaps this year, including a spate on aircraft carriers at sea and the collision between an Army helicopter and a passenger jet over Washington, D.C., in January, which killed 67 people.

Investigations found that the Black Hawk helicopter’s altimeter gauge was broken, there were issues with the military pilot's night vision goggles, and the Federal Aviation Administration didn't address warnings about the dangers that helicopters presented in the area around the Washington airport.

Unlike their civilian counterparts, military aviators face far less predictability and routine when they fly, Nance said.

“You’ve got aircraft commanders ... making decisions with the best information they’ve got, but on the spur of the moment and there’s a level of uncertainty and a level of unpredictability that is wildly beyond anything the commercial airlines experience,” he said.

In the spring, the Navy's USS Harry S. Truman aircraft carrier lost two F/A-18 Super Hornet fighter jets in the span of a few weeks — one to a bad landing and another slipped off the deck of the ship and fell into the sea.

In December 2024, the guided-missile cruiser USS Gettysburg mistakenly shot down an F/A-18 from the carrier.

No aviators were killed in any of these episodes. The Navy has not released the results of investigations into the causes of these mishaps.

More recently, four U.S. Army soldiers who were part of an elite team that does nighttime missions died when their Black Hawk helicopter crashed near a military base in Washington state while on a training mission in September.

Then, in October, a fighter jet and a helicopter based off the aircraft carrier USS Nimitz both crashed into the South China Sea within 30 minutes of each other, though no one was killed.

Nance didn't rule out the possibility that this spike in mishaps is the downstream effect of the COVID-19 pandemic, when military pilots had far less flying time.

“The safety buffer is impacted by a million things,” Nance said. Some things make tiny impacts and others are major. According to him, the pandemic “was a major impact on the operational capabilities.”

Warren's office is now asking for more detailed figures from the Pentagon on aviation mishaps and over a longer period of time, from 2019 to 2025, according to a request sent to the Pentagon and reviewed by AP. The request includes questions about Class A mishaps but asks for data on the less serious Class B and C mishaps as well.

Warren's office is also asking more questions about how the military trains its aircrews and maintenance staff.

## May 2024 Aviation Accident & Incident Summary

 Details  Published: 15 June 2024 

![Image 2](https://azpilots.org/images/news/safety/aviation_accident_summary_october_2018.jpg)

by Jim Timm

The following are the reports of aviation accidents and incidents that have occurred in Arizona from mid-April through May. We hope to use the following detailed accident information to develop safety programs, briefings, and posters/flyers that would help pilots learn from the mistakes being made by others and be able to take the necessary action to prevent them from having similar occurrences.

The number of accidents/Incidents have been very significantly up this past reporting period, and aviation safety has also not been the best because of a fatality that was incurred in one of the accidents. At least in all the other occurrences nobody got hurt. Things will have to improve as we go forward.

In continuing with the expanded scope of the report, we’re using information from the Aviation Safety Network (ASN), FAA, NTSB, and APA Members. This more inclusive information source suits our purpose of trying to get an idea of what is happening out there so we can help make flying safer.

In the meantime, here are the results from the above sources.

Date: **April 12, 2024**

Source: FAA, NTSB

Location: Wilcox

Type: Piper PA-28-32-300

Injuries: 3 Uninjured

by Jim Timm

We hope to use the following detailed accident information to develop safety programs, briefings, and posters/flyers that would help pilots learn from the mistakes being made by others and be able to take the necessary action to prevent them from having similar occurrences.

By [David Jack Kenny](https://www.ainonline.com/author/david-jack-kenny) • Contributor - Safety

May 1, 2024

# **Preliminary Reports**

## **One Killed, Five Hurt in North Sea Training Accident**

### Sikorsky S-92A, Feb. 28, 2024,15 nm west of Bergen, Norway

A search-and-rescue (SAR) crew located five of the six crew members after the helicopter crashed into the sea near Sotra Island but had to return to base for fuel before locating the sixth. By the time a second flight found her, the 61-year-old nurse had been in the water more than 25 minutes. She was pronounced dead on arrival at the hospital; one survivor was hospitalized in critical condition and a second was described as seriously hurt.

The wreckage was subsequently recovered from a depth of 220 meters (720 feet). Records retrieved from the flight data recorder led investigators to conclude that the crash “cannot be described as a controlled emergency landing,” possibly explaining why the aircraft’s emergency floats did not activate. The accident, which prompted a brief safety standdown, occurred while the crew was training to conduct SAR operations.

## **Five Perish in ILS Undershoot**

### IAI 1125 Westwind, March 10, 2024, Hot Springs, Virginia

Both pilots and all three passengers were killed when the twin-engine jet struck trees about 300 feet short of the threshold of Runway 25 of Ingalls Field Airport (KHSP). Although the operator, SkyJet Elite, held a Part 135 charter certificate, the trip from Florida’s Fort Lauderdale/Hollywood International Airport was filed as a personal flight under FAR Part 91.

The passengers had planned to attend a conference in Hot Springs while the crew was set to continue to Teterboro Airport in New Jersey.

At about 14:30 local time when the aircraft was 60 nm south of Hot Springs, the crew checked in with Washington Air Route Traffic Control Center and was instructed to inform on which instrument approach they wanted to use. At 14:32, a controller again asked about the approach and if they had the current weather and notams. The crew requested ILS approach to Runway 25 and said their weather information was about an hour old.

About 14:41, the flight crew advised they had the current weather and notams and a few minutes later were cleared to fly direct to the AHLER intersection, which was an initial fix for the ILS approach to Runway 25 about 10 nm northeast of the airport. The flight crew read back the clearance and requested radar vectors for the approach, but were subsequently told to proceed directly to AHLER and cleared for the approach. At 14:47 the flight crew advised that they would cancel their IFR flight plan once on the ground at Hot Springs with the flight service station, and ATC said that the crew could cancel with the controller on the ground. The ATC told the crew there was no traffic observed between their aircraft and the airport and advised them to switch to the common traffic advisory frequency (CTAF). The flight crew readback the instruction; it was the final communication with the controller.

An airport staff member heard the crew announce their intention to land over the CTAF. Shortly after, he heard the aircraft crash and saw smoke rising from the approach end of Runway 25.

The debris path was approximately in line with the runway centerline, oriented 250 to 255 degrees, and spanned 151 feet. Extensive impact damage precluded confirming flight control continuity. Investigators determined that the landing gear was down and flaps extended to 40 degrees; damage to both engines suggested they were operating until impact.

A weather observation recorded three minutes after the accident included winds from 280 degrees at 19 knots gusting to 38, 10 miles visibility, and scattered clouds at 2,000 feet beneath a 2,400-foot broken layer and a 4,500-foot overcast.

## **Few Clues about Cause of Hawker Fatal**

### Beechcraft Hawker 900XP, Feb. 7, 2024, Westwater, Utah

The National Transportation Safety Board’s (NTSB) preliminary report on the fatal accident contains details of the final flight. However, it sheds little light on what might have caused the twinjet to descend seemingly out of control and crash near Westwater, Utah. The two pilots were killed in the planned Part 91 IFR positioning flight from Grand Junction Regional Airport (KGJT), Colorado, to Gig Harbor, Washington.

The airplane, operated by Vici Aviation and managed by Clay Lacy Aviation, arrived at West Star Aviation’s facility at GJT on Dec. 20, 2023, for routine maintenance. According to West Star, multiple routine inspections had been completed on the airplane, including a requirement to remove the wing leading edges and TKS panels to inspect for cracks and signs of corrosion. After the inspections were completed, the airplane was returned to service on February 6.

During the positioning flight, the pilots planned to perform a stall warning and systems check per the airframe manufacturer’s requirements. These requirements, listed in the pilot’s operating manual, included an altitude above 10,000 feet agl, 10,000 feet above clouds, and below 18,000 feet msl. In addition, this check could be conducted only during day VMC with a good visual horizon, the autopilot disengaged, an operative stall warning system, the external surfaces free of ice, the ventral fuel tank empty, and weather radar on standby.

After the airplane departed GJT at 10:37 and entered a climb on a southeast heading, ATC approved the pilots’ request for a block of altitude from FL180 to FL200. At about 10:44, the aircraft leveled off at FL200. Three minutes later, ADS-B flight track data showed the airplane in a rapid descent in a circular pattern that resembled the shape of a corkscrew.

The airplane made multiple rotations before crashing into open terrain. The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder were recovered and the wreckage has also been retained for further examination. The accident site was IMC at the time of the accident.

# **Final Reports**

## **Pilot Inexperience Cited in Fatal Approach Crash**

### Piper PA-46-500TP, Nov. 9, 2022, Bignell, Nebraska

The NTSB identified the 505-hour private pilot’s “lack of total instrument experience” as having contributed to “spatial disorientation, loss of control, and an impact with terrain” during flight into low instrument conditions and turbulence.

The pilot and his only passenger were killed when the single-engine turboprop veered left from the course of the ILS approach to Runway 30 of the North Platte Regional Airport (KLBF), descending at a rate that eventually exceeded 5,000 fpm.

Prevailing conditions included a 300-foot overcast with light freezing drizzle; an Airmet for low-level wind shear was in effect for a 20-knot change in wind speed within 2,000 feet of the surface. Sounding data “indicated a high potential for moderate or greater turbulence between 3,600 and 5,500 feet msl” in a temperature inversion.

The 41-year-old pilot had purchased the airplane about three weeks earlier and received 10 hours of ground instruction and 15.1 hours of dual instruction in the accident airplane in the course of his transition training.

The instructor “gave the pilot a low average score at the completion of the training” which included 1.0 hour in actual instrument conditions encountered in the course of high-altitude instruction. He flew another 9.4 hours in the 12 days after completing transition training but had logged only 5.2 total hours in actual instrument conditions.

ADS-B track data showed that during the last minute of the flight the airplane’s descent rate increased from 500 to 3,000 fpm. In the last 30 seconds it entered a 2,000-fpm climb, then entered a descending left turn that exceeded 5,000 fpm. The pilot of a Cessna 208 freighter inbound from Omaha behind the accident flight recalled current weather reported as one to two miles visibility under a 200-foot overcast with light freezing rain.

He anticipated a “very demanding” approach with potential icing and a tailwind when landing on Runway 30 and acknowledged that the terminal area forecasts provided to himself and the accident pilot “were somewhat behind the actual reported weather conditions.” He flew two holding patterns before diverting to an airport farther south after that aircraft could not be located.

## **Glacier Impact Attributed to Flat Light**

### Bell 206L, June 28, 2023, Grise Fiord, Nunavut, Canada

Flat light conditions and featureless terrain were cited in the helicopter’s collision with a glacier in the Devon Ice Cap while attempting to drop markers to better define a landing zone. The pilot and both passengers, surveyors for the Polar Continental Shelf Program, escaped with minor injuries.

The accident occurred on the second attempt to land on the glacier, the pilot having broken off the first after determining that the surface was too indistinct for a safe landing approach. The helicopter returned to Truelove Inlet so the pilot could “make markers to drop onto the glacier to improve the surface definition at the landing area.”

The second flight departed at 10:18, flying in unrestricted visibility at an altitude of 3,800 feet under an overcast layer. The pilot crossed the glacier at an altitude of 75 feet to 100 feet, slowing the rotorcraft to about 30 knots.

After passing rocks serving as a reference point, the pilot lost visual contact with the surface and allowed the helicopter to enter a shallow descent, coming into contact with rising terrain in “a slight lateral motion to the right” that progressed to dynamic rollover. There was no fuel spill or post-impact fire, and after all three escaped the wreckage, a passenger was able to contact the program office in Resolute Bay via satellite phone. A rescue flight arrived two and a half hours later.

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada’s report notes that flat-light conditions can deprive pilots of both depth perception and contrast sensitivity, and scene photographs taken just after the accident confirm the lack of any definite horizon at the site.

By [David Jack Kenny](https://www.ainonline.com/author/david-jack-kenny) • Contributor - Safety

May 1, 2024

# **Preliminary Reports**

## **One Killed, Five Hurt in North Sea Training Accident**

### Sikorsky S-92A, Feb. 28, 2024,15 nm west of Bergen, Norway

A search-and-rescue (SAR) crew located five of the six crew members after the helicopter crashed into the sea near Sotra Island but had to return to base for fuel before locating the sixth. By the time a second flight found her, the 61-year-old nurse had been in the water more than 25 minutes. She was pronounced dead on arrival at the hospital; one survivor was hospitalized in critical condition and a second was described as seriously hurt.

The wreckage was subsequently recovered from a depth of 220 meters (720 feet). Records retrieved from the flight data recorder led investigators to conclude that the crash “cannot be described as a controlled emergency landing,” possibly explaining why the aircraft’s emergency floats did not activate. The accident, which prompted a brief safety standdown, occurred while the crew was training to conduct SAR operations.

## **Five Perish in ILS Undershoot**

### IAI 1125 Westwind, March 10, 2024, Hot Springs, Virginia

Both pilots and all three passengers were killed when the twin-engine jet struck trees about 300 feet short of the threshold of Runway 25 of Ingalls Field Airport (KHSP). Although the operator, SkyJet Elite, held a Part 135 charter certificate, the trip from Florida’s Fort Lauderdale/Hollywood International Airport was filed as a personal flight under FAR Part 91.

The passengers had planned to attend a conference in Hot Springs while the crew was set to continue to Teterboro Airport in New Jersey.

At about 14:30 local time when the aircraft was 60 nm south of Hot Springs, the crew checked in with Washington Air Route Traffic Control Center and was instructed to inform on which instrument approach they wanted to use. At 14:32, a controller again asked about the approach and if they had the current weather and notams. The crew requested ILS approach to Runway 25 and said their weather information was about an hour old.

About 14:41, the flight crew advised they had the current weather and notams and a few minutes later were cleared to fly direct to the AHLER intersection, which was an initial fix for the ILS approach to Runway 25 about 10 nm northeast of the airport. The flight crew read back the clearance and requested radar vectors for the approach, but were subsequently told to proceed directly to AHLER and cleared for the approach. At 14:47 the flight crew advised that they would cancel their IFR flight plan once on the ground at Hot Springs with the flight service station, and ATC said that the crew could cancel with the controller on the ground. The ATC told the crew there was no traffic observed between their aircraft and the airport and advised them to switch to the common traffic advisory frequency (CTAF). The flight crew readback the instruction; it was the final communication with the controller.

An airport staff member heard the crew announce their intention to land over the CTAF. Shortly after, he heard the aircraft crash and saw smoke rising from the approach end of Runway 25.

The debris path was approximately in line with the runway centerline, oriented 250 to 255 degrees, and spanned 151 feet. Extensive impact damage precluded confirming flight control continuity. Investigators determined that the landing gear was down and flaps extended to 40 degrees; damage to both engines suggested they were operating until impact.

A weather observation recorded three minutes after the accident included winds from 280 degrees at 19 knots gusting to 38, 10 miles visibility, and scattered clouds at 2,000 feet beneath a 2,400-foot broken layer and a 4,500-foot overcast.

## **Few Clues about Cause of Hawker Fatal**

### Beechcraft Hawker 900XP, Feb. 7, 2024, Westwater, Utah

The National Transportation Safety Board’s (NTSB) preliminary report on the fatal accident contains details of the final flight. However, it sheds little light on what might have caused the twinjet to descend seemingly out of control and crash near Westwater, Utah. The two pilots were killed in the planned Part 91 IFR positioning flight from Grand Junction Regional Airport (KGJT), Colorado, to Gig Harbor, Washington.

The airplane, operated by Vici Aviation and managed by Clay Lacy Aviation, arrived at West Star Aviation’s facility at GJT on Dec. 20, 2023, for routine maintenance. According to West Star, multiple routine inspections had been completed on the airplane, including a requirement to remove the wing leading edges and TKS panels to inspect for cracks and signs of corrosion. After the inspections were completed, the airplane was returned to service on February 6.

During the positioning flight, the pilots planned to perform a stall warning and systems check per the airframe manufacturer’s requirements. These requirements, listed in the pilot’s operating manual, included an altitude above 10,000 feet agl, 10,000 feet above clouds, and below 18,000 feet msl. In addition, this check could be conducted only during day VMC with a good visual horizon, the autopilot disengaged, an operative stall warning system, the external surfaces free of ice, the ventral fuel tank empty, and weather radar on standby.

After the airplane departed GJT at 10:37 and entered a climb on a southeast heading, ATC approved the pilots’ request for a block of altitude from FL180 to FL200. At about 10:44, the aircraft leveled off at FL200. Three minutes later, ADS-B flight track data showed the airplane in a rapid descent in a circular pattern that resembled the shape of a corkscrew.

The airplane made multiple rotations before crashing into open terrain. The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder were recovered and the wreckage has also been retained for further examination. The accident site was IMC at the time of the accident.

# **Final Reports**

## **Pilot Inexperience Cited in Fatal Approach Crash**

### Piper PA-46-500TP, Nov. 9, 2022, Bignell, Nebraska

The NTSB identified the 505-hour private pilot’s “lack of total instrument experience” as having contributed to “spatial disorientation, loss of control, and an impact with terrain” during flight into low instrument conditions and turbulence.

The pilot and his only passenger were killed when the single-engine turboprop veered left from the course of the ILS approach to Runway 30 of the North Platte Regional Airport (KLBF), descending at a rate that eventually exceeded 5,000 fpm.

Prevailing conditions included a 300-foot overcast with light freezing drizzle; an Airmet for low-level wind shear was in effect for a 20-knot change in wind speed within 2,000 feet of the surface. Sounding data “indicated a high potential for moderate or greater turbulence between 3,600 and 5,500 feet msl” in a temperature inversion.

The 41-year-old pilot had purchased the airplane about three weeks earlier and received 10 hours of ground instruction and 15.1 hours of dual instruction in the accident airplane in the course of his transition training.

The instructor “gave the pilot a low average score at the completion of the training” which included 1.0 hour in actual instrument conditions encountered in the course of high-altitude instruction. He flew another 9.4 hours in the 12 days after completing transition training but had logged only 5.2 total hours in actual instrument conditions.

ADS-B track data showed that during the last minute of the flight the airplane’s descent rate increased from 500 to 3,000 fpm. In the last 30 seconds it entered a 2,000-fpm climb, then entered a descending left turn that exceeded 5,000 fpm. The pilot of a Cessna 208 freighter inbound from Omaha behind the accident flight recalled current weather reported as one to two miles visibility under a 200-foot overcast with light freezing rain.

He anticipated a “very demanding” approach with potential icing and a tailwind when landing on Runway 30 and acknowledged that the terminal area forecasts provided to himself and the accident pilot “were somewhat behind the actual reported weather conditions.” He flew two holding patterns before diverting to an airport farther south after that aircraft could not be located.

## **Glacier Impact Attributed to Flat Light**

### Bell 206L, June 28, 2023, Grise Fiord, Nunavut, Canada

Flat light conditions and featureless terrain were cited in the helicopter’s collision with a glacier in the Devon Ice Cap while attempting to drop markers to better define a landing zone. The pilot and both passengers, surveyors for the Polar Continental Shelf Program, escaped with minor injuries.

The accident occurred on the second attempt to land on the glacier, the pilot having broken off the first after determining that the surface was too indistinct for a safe landing approach. The helicopter returned to Truelove Inlet so the pilot could “make markers to drop onto the glacier to improve the surface definition at the landing area.”

The second flight departed at 10:18, flying in unrestricted visibility at an altitude of 3,800 feet under an overcast layer. The pilot crossed the glacier at an altitude of 75 feet to 100 feet, slowing the rotorcraft to about 30 knots.

After passing rocks serving as a reference point, the pilot lost visual contact with the surface and allowed the helicopter to enter a shallow descent, coming into contact with rising terrain in “a slight lateral motion to the right” that progressed to dynamic rollover. There was no fuel spill or post-impact fire, and after all three escaped the wreckage, a passenger was able to contact the program office in Resolute Bay via satellite phone. A rescue flight arrived two and a half hours later.

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada’s report notes that flat-light conditions can deprive pilots of both depth perception and contrast sensitivity, and scene photographs taken just after the accident confirm the lack of any definite horizon at the site.

FLUVANNA COUNTY, Va. (WSET) — Two people are dead after a plane crashed in Virginia Sunday morning, according to officials.

Around 9 a.m. on May 5, residents in Fluvanna County reported hearing a low-flying plane followed by an explosion, Virginia State Police said.

Law enforcement and first responders turned out to an area off of Miles Jackson Road to look for the impact site, police said. During the search, officials found a burning aircraft in a forested area.

![Image 9: First responders and law enforcement responded to the scene of the Fluvanna County plane crash. (Virginia State Police)](https://wset.com/resources/media2/16x9/full/800/center/80/5ed63979-7b36-4381-939e-b0568f839641-medium16x9_IMG_92831.JPG)

First responders and law enforcement responded to the scene of the Fluvanna County plane crash. (Virginia State Police)

At that point, the Fluvanna County Sheriff's Office, Virginia Conservation Police and Virginia State Police were all responding to the scene. When the plane was found, fire crews from the area worked together to put out the flames.

**SEE ALSO: [Woman dies after being trapped under lawn mower in drainage ravine](https://wset.com/news/nation-world/woman-dies-after-being-trapped-under-lawn-mower-in-drainage-ravine#)**

VSP said their office was able to identify both the pilot and a single passenger of the plane, but neither survived the crash.

"The privately owned, twin-engine 1975 Rockwell Aero Commander 690A was being piloted by John W. Latham, 63, of Haymarket, Va.," VSP said. "Neither Latham nor his passenger, Niiben C.A. Ayivorh, 73, of Burke, Va., survived the crash."

![Image 10: Virginia State Police said the airplane was found crashed and burning in dense woods in Fluvanna County. (Virginia State Police)](https://wset.com/resources/media2/16x9/full/800/center/80/fe561145-6b55-485a-bdb1-39d2a2c65b7f-medium16x9_IMG_92851.JPG)

Virginia State Police said the airplane was found crashed and burning in dense woods in Fluvanna County. (Virginia State Police)

Police said the plane had been headed toward Georgetown, S.C. after leaving Manassas Regional Airport that morning.

The remains of the pilot and passenger were taken to the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner in Richmond for an examination and autopsy. VSP said both the FAA and NTSB were notified about the crash.

The NTSB said they are trying to find missing parts from the plane and are asking for help with recovery in a statement.

"The National Transportation Safety Board is seeking assistance with the recovery of an engine, propeller and other airframe parts that separated from an airplane that crashed near Palmyra, Virginia, in Fluvanna County on Sunday morning," NTSB said. "The Rockwell Commander 690 was flying north to south on a route near Miles Jackson Road when parts started to separate from the airplane. Some airplane parts have already been recovered in that area in a debris field that stretches to nearly three miles."

FLUVANNA COUNTY, Va. (WSET) — Two people are dead after a plane crashed in Virginia Sunday morning, according to officials.

Around 9 a.m. on May 5, residents in Fluvanna County reported hearing a low-flying plane followed by an explosion, Virginia State Police said.

Law enforcement and first responders turned out to an area off of Miles Jackson Road to look for the impact site, police said. During the search, officials found a burning aircraft in a forested area.

![Image 9: First responders and law enforcement responded to the scene of the Fluvanna County plane crash. (Virginia State Police)](https://wset.com/resources/media2/16x9/full/800/center/80/5ed63979-7b36-4381-939e-b0568f839641-medium16x9_IMG_92831.JPG)

First responders and law enforcement responded to the scene of the Fluvanna County plane crash. (Virginia State Police)

At that point, the Fluvanna County Sheriff's Office, Virginia Conservation Police and Virginia State Police were all responding to the scene. When the plane was found, fire crews from the area worked together to put out the flames.

**SEE ALSO: [Woman dies after being trapped under lawn mower in drainage ravine](https://wset.com/news/nation-world/woman-dies-after-being-trapped-under-lawn-mower-in-drainage-ravine#)**

VSP said their office was able to identify both the pilot and a single passenger of the plane, but neither survived the crash.

"The privately owned, twin-engine 1975 Rockwell Aero Commander 690A was being piloted by John W. Latham, 63, of Haymarket, Va.," VSP said. "Neither Latham nor his passenger, Niiben C.A. Ayivorh, 73, of Burke, Va., survived the crash."

![Image 10: Virginia State Police said the airplane was found crashed and burning in dense woods in Fluvanna County. (Virginia State Police)](https://wset.com/resources/media2/16x9/full/800/center/80/fe561145-6b55-485a-bdb1-39d2a2c65b7f-medium16x9_IMG_92851.JPG)

Virginia State Police said the airplane was found crashed and burning in dense woods in Fluvanna County. (Virginia State Police)

Police said the plane had been headed toward Georgetown, S.C. after leaving Manassas Regional Airport that morning.

The remains of the pilot and passenger were taken to the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner in Richmond for an examination and autopsy. VSP said both the FAA and NTSB were notified about the crash.

The NTSB said they are trying to find missing parts from the plane and are asking for help with recovery in a statement.

"The National Transportation Safety Board is seeking assistance with the recovery of an engine, propeller and other airframe parts that separated from an airplane that crashed near Palmyra, Virginia, in Fluvanna County on Sunday morning," NTSB said. "The Rockwell Commander 690 was flying north to south on a route near Miles Jackson Road when parts started to separate from the airplane. Some airplane parts have already been recovered in that area in a debris field that stretches to nearly three miles."

# Federal authorities investigate near-collision of two planes at Virginia airport

This article is more than 2 years old

American Airlines plane forced to abort takeoff at Ronald Reagan Washington national airport as another flight cleared for landing

[Maya Yang](https://www.theguardian.com/profile/maya-yang)

Thu 30 May 2024 13.40 EDT Last modified on Thu 30 May 2024 14.03 EDT

Share

[Prefer the Guardian on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=theguardian.com)

The Federal Aviation Administration is investigating an incident at Ronald Reagan Washington national airport in which a plane was forced to brake to narrowly avoid a collision with another plane, the second near-collision at the airport in less than two months.

At around 10.20am on Wednesday, Boston-bound American Airlines flight 2134, carrying approximately 100 passengers and crew, was cleared for takeoff and began to accelerate.

[![Image 3: American Airlines planes at an airport](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/b447b3180a8e615bc2230e68b684529a7b9d6338/0_286_7781_4670/master/7781.jpg?width=460&quality=85&auto=format&fit=max&s=d621ee2b5c8508106c89abf57ead6396) Lawsuit claims American Airlines asked Black passengers to deboard flight Read more](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/article/2024/may/29/american-airlines-black-passenger-discrimination-lawsuit)

The plane was then forced to abort as it was scheduled at the same time as another plane, a private King Air flight, was cleared to land on an intersecting runway.

The American Airlines plane had been traveling up to 100mph when it was ordered to break immediately, NBC 10 [reports](https://www.nbcboston.com/news/local/boston-bound-flight-averts-runway-collision-at-reagan-national-airport/3384166/).

In air traffic controller recordings obtained by the outlet, an air traffic controller can be heard [saying](https://www.nbcboston.com/news/local/boston-bound-flight-averts-runway-collision-at-reagan-national-airport/3384166/): “American 2134, cancel takeoff clearance! Zero, Alpha, Alpha, go around, go around!”

“Rejecting the takeoff, 2134,” another voice said.

“Zero, Alpha, Alpha cannot go around, we were already on the ground,” someone who appeared to be the pilot from the King Air plane said.

In a statement an FAA spokesperson [said](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/faa-investigating-collision-ronald-reagan-washington-national-airport-rcna154627): “An air traffic controller canceled the takeoff clearance for American Airlines Flight 2134 because another aircraft was cleared to land on an intersecting runway at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.”

American Airlines [said](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/faa-investigating-collision-ronald-reagan-washington-national-airport-rcna154627) it was working alongside the FAA in its investigation, adding, “The safety of our customers and team members is our top priority, and we’re grateful to our crew for their professionalism.”

The Virginia Democratic senator Tim Kaine [tweeted](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/faa-investigating-collision-ronald-reagan-washington-national-airport-rcna154627): “I’m relieved no one was hurt. But this incident underscores again that DCA [Ronald Reagan Washington national airport] is at capacity. This shows why Senate action to jam even more flights into DCA was so dangerous. The FAA must resist any new flights that compromise safety.”

Wednesday’s incident marks the airport’s second near-collision in six weeks.

On 18 April, a Southwest Airlines plane and nearly collided with a JetBlue plane after an air traffic controller instructed it to cross the runway while the JetBlue plane was getting ready to take off.

No injuries were reported and the FAA said at the time it would [investigate](https://www.dallasnews.com/business/airlines/2024/04/19/southwest-airlines-jetblue-planes-nearly-collide-at-reagan-national-airport/).

A slew of issues have beset the global aviation industry in recent months. Last week, one passenger died and dozens were injured following intense [turbulence](https://www.theguardian.com/world/video/2024/may/21/passengers-carried-off-singapore-airlines-plane-severe-turbulence-video-report) on a Singapore Airlines flight heading from London to Singapore. A few days later, eight people were [hospitalized](https://www.theguardian.com/world/article/2024/may/26/turbulence-on-qatar-airways-flight-from-doha-to-dublin) following another bout of turbulence on a Qatar Airways flight from Doha to Dublin.

In March, United Airlines had at least four safety [incidents](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2024/mar/09/united-emergency-landing-los-angeles) within a week, with flights being forced to make emergency diversions due to issues with hydraulic systems, planes rolling off taxiways and on to grassy lawns and a tire falling off mid-flight.

The Federal Aviation Administration is investigating an incident at Ronald Reagan Washington national airport in which a plane was forced to brake to narrowly avoid a collision with another plane, the second near-collision at the airport in less than two months.

At around 10.20am on Wednesday, Boston-bound American Airlines flight 2134, carrying approximately 100 passengers and crew, was cleared for takeoff and began to accelerate.

[![Image 3: American Airlines planes at an airport](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/b447b3180a8e615bc2230e68b684529a7b9d6338/0_286_7781_4670/master/7781.jpg?width=460&quality=85&auto=format&fit=max&s=d621ee2b5c8508106c89abf57ead6396) Lawsuit claims American Airlines asked Black passengers to deboard flight Read more](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/article/2024/may/29/american-airlines-black-passenger-discrimination-lawsuit)

The plane was then forced to abort as it was scheduled at the same time as another plane, a private King Air flight, was cleared to land on an intersecting runway.

The American Airlines plane had been traveling up to 100mph when it was ordered to break immediately, NBC 10 [reports](https://www.nbcboston.com/news/local/boston-bound-flight-averts-runway-collision-at-reagan-national-airport/3384166/).

In air traffic controller recordings obtained by the outlet, an air traffic controller can be heard [saying](https://www.nbcboston.com/news/local/boston-bound-flight-averts-runway-collision-at-reagan-national-airport/3384166/): “American 2134, cancel takeoff clearance! Zero, Alpha, Alpha, go around, go around!”

“Rejecting the takeoff, 2134,” another voice said.

“Zero, Alpha, Alpha cannot go around, we were already on the ground,” someone who appeared to be the pilot from the King Air plane said.

In a statement an FAA spokesperson [said](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/faa-investigating-collision-ronald-reagan-washington-national-airport-rcna154627): “An air traffic controller canceled the takeoff clearance for American Airlines Flight 2134 because another aircraft was cleared to land on an intersecting runway at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.”

American Airlines [said](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/faa-investigating-collision-ronald-reagan-washington-national-airport-rcna154627) it was working alongside the FAA in its investigation, adding, “The safety of our customers and team members is our top priority, and we’re grateful to our crew for their professionalism.”

The Virginia Democratic senator Tim Kaine [tweeted](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/faa-investigating-collision-ronald-reagan-washington-national-airport-rcna154627): “I’m relieved no one was hurt. But this incident underscores again that DCA [Ronald Reagan Washington national airport] is at capacity. This shows why Senate action to jam even more flights into DCA was so dangerous. The FAA must resist any new flights that compromise safety.”

Wednesday’s incident marks the airport’s second near-collision in six weeks.

On 18 April, a Southwest Airlines plane and nearly collided with a JetBlue plane after an air traffic controller instructed it to cross the runway while the JetBlue plane was getting ready to take off.

No injuries were reported and the FAA said at the time it would [investigate](https://www.dallasnews.com/business/airlines/2024/04/19/southwest-airlines-jetblue-planes-nearly-collide-at-reagan-national-airport/).

A slew of issues have beset the global aviation industry in recent months. Last week, one passenger died and dozens were injured following intense [turbulence](https://www.theguardian.com/world/video/2024/may/21/passengers-carried-off-singapore-airlines-plane-severe-turbulence-video-report) on a Singapore Airlines flight heading from London to Singapore. A few days later, eight people were [hospitalized](https://www.theguardian.com/world/article/2024/may/26/turbulence-on-qatar-airways-flight-from-doha-to-dublin) following another bout of turbulence on a Qatar Airways flight from Doha to Dublin.

In March, United Airlines had at least four safety [incidents](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2024/mar/09/united-emergency-landing-los-angeles) within a week, with flights being forced to make emergency diversions due to issues with hydraulic systems, planes rolling off taxiways and on to grassy lawns and a tire falling off mid-flight.

### January

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_aviation&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: January")]

2 January A runway collision at [Haneda Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haneda_Airport "Haneda Airport") in Tokyo occurred when [Japan Airlines Flight 516](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Haneda_Airport_runway_collision "2024 Haneda Airport runway collision"), operated by an [Airbus A350-900](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airbus_A350-900 "Airbus A350-900") arriving from [Sapporo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Chitose_Airport "New Chitose Airport"), collided with a [Japan Coast Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Coast_Guard "Japan Coast Guard") aircraft and both aircraft caught on fire. This resulted in the complete destruction of both aircraft. All 367 passengers and 12 crew members of the Airbus were evacuated. There were six occupants on board the Coast Guard aircraft, a [De Havilland Canada Dash 8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Havilland_Canada_Dash_8 "De Havilland Canada Dash 8"); the captain escaped with serious injuries whilst the remaining five crew members were killed. This was the first hull loss of an A350. The Coast Guard aircraft was scheduled to provide relief to [Niigata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niigata_Prefecture "Niigata Prefecture") in response to the previous day's [Noto Peninsula earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Noto_earthquake "2024 Noto earthquake").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-HanadaAirportRunwayCollision1-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-HanadaAirportRunwayCollision2-2)5 January Shortly after departing [Portland International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_International_Airport "Portland International Airport") in Oregon, a [Boeing 737 MAX 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_737_MAX "Boeing 737 MAX") operating as [Alaska Airlines Flight 1282](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_Airlines_Flight_1282 "Alaska Airlines Flight 1282") suffered an explosive decompression when a plug covering an unused exit door blew out. The aircraft made a safe return to Portland with all 177 occupants alive.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-3) The [FAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FAA "FAA") subsequently ordered all 737 MAX 9 planes fitted with door plugs to be grounded for inspection.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-4) It was subsequently reported that Alaska Airlines and United Airlines both discovered faults on other 737s.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-5)12 January An [autonomous underwater vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_underwater_vehicle "Autonomous underwater vehicle") – developed by the [National Institute of Ocean Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institute_of_Ocean_Technology "National Institute of Ocean Technology") and launched with the aim of finding the wreckage of an [Indian Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Air_Force "Indian Air Force")[Antonov An-26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonov_An-26 "Antonov An-26") that [disappeared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Indian_Air_Force_An-32_crash "2016 Indian Air Force An-32 crash") over the [Bay of Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Bengal "Bay of Bengal") on 22 July 2016 – located the wreckage of the aircraft 310 kilometres (190 mi) off the [Chennai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chennai "Chennai") coast.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-8)Following [airstrikes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_missile_strikes_in_Yemen "2024 missile strikes in Yemen") conducted by the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") against [Houthi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houthi "Houthi")-held [Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemen "Yemen"), the [Federal Air Transport Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Air_Transport_Agency "Federal Air Transport Agency") banned Russian airlines from flying through Yemeni airspace until further notice.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-10)16 January The [United States Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice") blocked the proposed $3.8 billion acquisition of [Spirit Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_Airlines "Spirit Airlines") by [JetBlue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JetBlue "JetBlue"), citing that it would create a lack of competition in [low-cost carriers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-cost_carrier "Low-cost carrier"). The [stock price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_price "Stock price") of Spirit Airlines dropped by 47% after the decision was ### February

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_aviation&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: February")]

6 February A [Robinson R44 Raven II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinson_R44_Raven_II "Robinson R44 Raven II") helicopter piloted by former Chilean president [Sebastián Piñera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebasti%C3%A1n_Pi%C3%B1era "Sebastián Piñera") lost control and [crashed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_and_state_funeral_of_Sebasti%C3%A1n_Pi%C3%B1era#Accident "Death and state funeral of Sebastián Piñera") into [Lake Ranco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Ranco "Lake Ranco") in Chile. Piñera was killed and the other three people on board survived.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-16)9 February A [Bombardier Challenger 600](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombardier_Challenger_600 "Bombardier Challenger 600") operating as [Hop-A-Jet Flight 823](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hop-A-Jet_Flight_823 "Hop-A-Jet Flight 823") crashed into a vehicle on Interstate 75 in [Collier County, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collier_County,_Florida "Collier County, Florida") while attempting to make an [emergency landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_landing "Emergency landing"). Two of the five on board were killed in the crash.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-17)A [Eurocopter EC130](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurocopter_EC130 "Eurocopter EC130")[crashed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Orbic_Air_Eurocopter_EC130_crash "2024 Orbic Air Eurocopter EC130 crash"), killing all six occupants, including Nigerian banker [Herbert Wigwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Wigwe "Herbert Wigwe").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-18)11 February The [United States Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice") seized a [Boeing 747-300](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_747 "Boeing 747") registered as YV3531 belonging to Venezuelan state-owned airline [Emtrasur Cargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emtrasur_Cargo "Emtrasur Cargo"). The DOJ said that the aircraft was sold to Emtrasur Cargo by [Mahan Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahan_Air "Mahan Air"),[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-AP_US_Seizes_747-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-Ch-aviation_US_DOJ-20) a sanctioned Iranian airline due to its affiliation with the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_Revolutionary_Guard_Corps "Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps"),[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-21) which was in violation of American export control laws. The aircraft was initially detained by Argentina on 6 June 2022, shortly after the United States had issued a seizure warrant.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-AP_US_Seizes_747-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-Ch-aviation_US_DOJ-20) The aircraft was subsequently scrapped at [Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dade-Collier_Training_and_Transition_Airport "Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-23)18 February[Air Serbia Flight 324](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Serbia_Flight_324 "Air Serbia Flight 324"), an [Embraer 195](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embraer_195 "Embraer 195") operated by [Marathon Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_Airlines "Marathon Airlines"), struck landing lights on takeoff at Belgrade [Nikola Tesla Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikola_Tesla_Airport "Nikola Tesla Airport"). The aircraft flew for another hour before making an [emergency landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_landing "Emergency landing") at the same airport with a gaping hole in the [fuselage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuselage "Fuselage"). All 111 occupants were reported safe.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-25)20–25 February The [Singapore Airshow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore_Airshow "Singapore Airshow") was held.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-26) Highlights included orders for Airbus from [Vietjet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietjet "Vietjet") (20 [A330neos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A330neo "A330neo")) and [Starlux Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starlux_Airlines "Starlux Airlines") (three A330neos and five [A350Fs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A350#A350-1000F "A350")), Boeing from [Thai Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_Airways_International "Thai Airways International") (45 [787-9s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/787-9 "787-9")) and [Royal Brunei Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Brunei_Airlines "Royal Brunei Airlines") (four 787-9s), and Comac from [Tibet Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet_Airlines "Tibet Airlines") (40 [C919s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C919 "C919") and 10 [ARJ21s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARJ21 "ARJ21")).[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-27)21 February The [TAI TF Kaan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TAI_TF_Kaan "TAI TF Kaan"), a fifth-gen stealth fighter being developed by [Turkish Aerospace Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_Aerospace_Industries "Turkish Aerospace Industries"), performed its maiden flight.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-auto2-28)26 February[Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian "Canadian") Budget airline [Lynx Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynx_Air "Lynx Air") ceased operations due to financial issues.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-cease-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-auto6-30)

### March

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_aviation&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: March")]

5 March A [Dash 8-300](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DHC-8-300 "DHC-8-300") operating as [Safarilink Aviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safarilink_Aviation "Safarilink Aviation") Flight 53 from [Wilson Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Airport "Wilson Airport"), Nairobi to [Diani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukunda_Airport "Ukunda Airport") near [Mombasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombasa "Mombasa") was involved in a [mid-air collision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safarilink_Aviation_Flight_053 "Safarilink Aviation Flight 053") with a [Cessna 172](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cessna_172 "Cessna 172") operated by a local flying school. The Dash returned to Wilson and landed safely with no injuries among the 39 passengers and 5 crew. The Cessna crashed in [Nairobi National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi_National_Park "Nairobi National Park") killing the two occupants.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-31)8 March[David E. Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_E._Harris "David E. Harris"), the first African American pilot who flew for a [major airline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Airlines "American Airlines"), died at the age of 89.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-Blair_2024_n061-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-33)10 March A [Boeing 787-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_787-9 "Boeing 787-9") operating as [LATAM Airlines Flight 800](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LATAM_Airlines_Flight_800 "LATAM Airlines Flight 800") experienced an in-flight [upset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_upset "Aircraft upset"), injuring 50 of the 272 occupants on board the aircraft. The plane made an [emergency landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_landing "Emergency landing") at [Auckland Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Airport "Auckland Airport").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-35)12 March A Russian [Ilyushin Il-76](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilyushin_Il-76 "Ilyushin Il-76") military transport aircraft [crashed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Ivanovo_Ilyushin_Il-76_crash "2024 Ivanovo Ilyushin Il-76 crash") near [Belgorod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgorod "Belgorod") after suffering an engine fire. All 15 on board were killed.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-37)In response to Argentina's role in the seizure of a Venezuelan state-owned [Emtrasur Cargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emtrasur_Cargo "Emtrasur Cargo")[Boeing 747-300](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_747 "Boeing 747") registered as YV3531 by the [DOJ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice"), Venezuela closed its airspace to Argentine aircraft. The [Venezuelan Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venezuelan_Government "Venezuelan Government") stated that the airspace would remain blocked until Argentina compensated the country.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-39)22 March The [Boom XB-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boom_XB-1 "Boom XB-1"), a prototype/technology demonstrator supersonic aircraft developed by [Boom Supersonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boom_Supersonic "Boom Supersonic"), conducts its first flight from [Mojave Air and Space Port](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mojave_Air_and_Space_Port "Mojave Air and Space Port"). The flight reaches a maximum altitude of 7,120 feet (2,170 m) and a top speed of 246 knots (456 km/h; 283 mph) during its 12-minute flight.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-auto1-40) The company aims to use the XB-1 to develop its [Overture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boom_Overture "Boom Overture")[supersonic airliner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersonic_transport "Supersonic transport"), of which the XB-1 is a roughly 1/3rd scale model.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-41)29 March In response to Venezuela's airspace closure to Argentina, the [Argentine Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentine_Government "Argentine Government") and [United States Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Government "United States Government") lodges a complaint to the [International Civil Aviation Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Civil_Aviation_Organization "International Civil Aviation Organization") (ICAO) to protest the closure, requesting that the airspace be reopened as a violation of the [Chicago Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Convention "Chicago Convention").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-43)

### April

4 April US company Skydweller Aero completes the world's first [unmanned flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unmanned_aerial_vehicle "Unmanned aerial vehicle") of a large solar-powered aircraft.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-44)13 April[Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq "Iraq"), [Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan "Jordan"), [Lebanon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanon "Lebanon"), [Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syria "Syria"), [Kuwait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuwait "Kuwait") and [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel") all close their airspaces in response to the [Iranian strikes in Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_2024_Iranian_strikes_against_Israel "April 2024 Iranian strikes against Israel").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-46)17 April The [FAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FAA "FAA") implements a [ground stop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ground_stop "Ground stop") for [Alaska Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_Airlines "Alaska Airlines") and its subsidiary [Horizon Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horizon_Air "Horizon Air") (meaning planes are not permitted to take off) after a notification by the airline. Alaska Airlines makes the request after an issue surfaced during a routine system upgrade essential for ensuring [aircraft weight and balance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_of_gravity_of_an_aircraft "Center of gravity of an aircraft"), although the exact nature of the issue is not disclosed. The airline states that it acted "out of an abundance of caution".[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-47)18 April Kenya's highest ranking military officer, [General Francis Ogolla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Omondi_Ogolla "Francis Omondi Ogolla"), and nine other members of the [Kenya Defence Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Defence_Forces "Kenya Defence Forces") are killed in the crash of a [UH-1 Huey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_UH-1_Iroquois "Bell UH-1 Iroquois") in western Kenya.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-49)23 April Two [Royal Malaysian Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Malaysian_Navy "Royal Malaysian Navy") helicopters [collide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Lumut_mid-air_collision "2024 Lumut mid-air collision") over [Lumut, Perak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lumut,_Perak "Lumut, Perak") in [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia") during a formation flight as part of a rehearsal for the upcoming Navy day parade. All 10 people on board the [Leonardo AW139](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_AW139 "Leonardo AW139") and [Eurocopter Fennec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurocopter_Fennec "Eurocopter Fennec") are killed.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-51)An Alaska Air Fuel [Douglas C-54D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_C-54D "Douglas C-54D")[crashed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Alaska_Air_Fuel_Douglas_C-54_crash "2024 Alaska Air Fuel Douglas C-54 crash") shortly after takeoff from [Fairbanks International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairbanks_International_Airport "Fairbanks International Airport"). Both pilots, the only people on board, are killed.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-52)25 April[Southwest Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Airlines "Southwest Airlines") and [American Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Airlines "American Airlines") report large first-quarter economic losses, with Southwest losing US$231 million and American expecting to lay off over 2,000 employees during the remainder of the year. In addition, Southwest is to stop flying to [Cozumel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cozumel_International_Airport "Cozumel International Airport"), [Syracuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syracuse_Hancock_International_Airport "Syracuse Hancock International Airport") and [Bellingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellingham_International_Airport "Bellingham International Airport") airports. These declines have limited the airlines' abilities to order more aircraft in the near future, with Southwest cancelling some of its [Boeing 737](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_737 "Boeing 737") orders for the year.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-53)30 April Australian low-cost airline [Bonza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonza "Bonza") which launched operations in January 2023, enters [voluntary administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voluntary_administration "Voluntary administration") with all services suspended.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-auto-54)

## Aviation safety

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_aviation&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Aviation safety")]

In 2015, the all-accident rate was equal to 1.75 per one million flights; in 2024, this number decreased to 1.13. Compared to 2023 in which there were 72 onboard fatalities, 2024 experienced seven fatal commercial accidents and recorded a significant increase of onboard fatalities including 244 onboard deaths with 7 other deaths listed as "other". The surge in fatalities was linked to the crash of [Jeju Air Flight 2216](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeju_Air_Flight_2216 "Jeju Air Flight 2216") in December 2024.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPriyadarshiKhareUpmanMandal20255-128)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIATA20256-129) 2024 marked the deadliest year in commercial aviation since 2018.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-130)

In 2024, the [International Air Transport Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Air_Transport_Association "International Air Transport Association") (IATA) recorded over 430,000 cases of [GNSS jamming and spoofing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GNSS_jamming "GNSS jamming"). Most of the recorded cases occurred around conflict zones and were mostly related to military activities.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPriyadarshiKhareUpmanMandal20255-128)

## Deadliest crash

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_aviation&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Deadliest crash")]

The deadliest crash in 2024 occurred when [Jeju Air Flight 2216](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeju_Air_Flight_2216 "Jeju Air Flight 2216"), a [Boeing 737-800](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_737-800 "Boeing 737-800"), [overran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runway_excursion "Runway excursion") the runway while performing a [belly landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belly_landing "Belly landing") in [Muan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muan_International_Airport "Muan International Airport"), South Korea, on 29 December, killing 179 of the 181 passengers and crew on board.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-131)

This is a list of aviation-related events in 2024.

## Events

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_aviation&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Events")]

### January

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_aviation&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: January")]

2 January A runway collision at [Haneda Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haneda_Airport "Haneda Airport") in Tokyo occurred when [Japan Airlines Flight 516](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Haneda_Airport_runway_collision "2024 Haneda Airport runway collision"), operated by an [Airbus A350-900](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airbus_A350-900 "Airbus A350-900") arriving from [Sapporo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Chitose_Airport "New Chitose Airport"), collided with a [Japan Coast Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Coast_Guard "Japan Coast Guard") aircraft and both aircraft caught on fire. This resulted in the complete destruction of both aircraft. All 367 passengers and 12 crew members of the Airbus were evacuated. There were six occupants on board the Coast Guard aircraft, a [De Havilland Canada Dash 8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Havilland_Canada_Dash_8 "De Havilland Canada Dash 8"); the captain escaped with serious injuries whilst the remaining five crew members were killed. This was the first hull loss of an A350. The Coast Guard aircraft was scheduled to provide relief to [Niigata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niigata_Prefecture "Niigata Prefecture") in response to the previous day's [Noto Peninsula earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Noto_earthquake "2024 Noto earthquake").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-HanadaAirportRunwayCollision1-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-HanadaAirportRunwayCollision2-2)5 January Shortly after departing [Portland International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_International_Airport "Portland International Airport") in Oregon, a [Boeing 737 MAX 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_737_MAX "Boeing 737 MAX") operating as [Alaska Airlines Flight 1282](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_Airlines_Flight_1282 "Alaska Airlines Flight 1282") suffered an explosive decompression when a plug covering an unused exit door blew out. The aircraft made a safe return to Portland with all 177 occupants alive.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-3) The [FAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FAA "FAA") subsequently ordered all 737 MAX 9 planes fitted with door plugs to be grounded for inspection.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-4) It was subsequently reported that Alaska Airlines and United Airlines both discovered faults on other 737s.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-5)12 January An [autonomous underwater vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_underwater_vehicle "Autonomous underwater vehicle") – developed by the [National Institute of Ocean Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institute_of_Ocean_Technology "National Institute of Ocean Technology") and launched with the aim of finding the wreckage of an [Indian Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Air_Force "Indian Air Force")[Antonov An-26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonov_An-26 "Antonov An-26") that [disappeared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Indian_Air_Force_An-32_crash "2016 Indian Air Force An-32 crash") over the [Bay of Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Bengal "Bay of Bengal") on 22 July 2016 – located the wreckage of the aircraft 310 kilometres (190 mi) off the [Chennai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chennai "Chennai") coast.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-8)Following and the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") against [Houthi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houthi "Houthi")-held [Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemen ### February

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_aviation&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: February")]

6 February A [Robinson R44 Raven II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinson_R44_Raven_II "Robinson R44 Raven II") helicopter piloted by former Chilean president [Sebastián Piñera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebasti%C3%A1n_Pi%C3%B1era "Sebastián Piñera") lost control and [crashed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_and_state_funeral_of_Sebasti%C3%A1n_Pi%C3%B1era#Accident "Death and state funeral of Sebastián Piñera") into [Lake Ranco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Ranco "Lake Ranco") in Chile. Piñera was killed and the other three people on board survived.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-16)9 February A [Bombardier Challenger 600](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombardier_Challenger_600 "Bombardier Challenger 600") operating as [Hop-A-Jet Flight 823](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hop-A-Jet_Flight_823 "Hop-A-Jet Flight 823") crashed into a vehicle on Interstate 75 in [Collier County, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collier_County,_Florida "Collier County, Florida") while attempting to make an [emergency landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_landing "Emergency landing"). Two of the five on board were killed in the crash.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-17)A [Eurocopter EC130](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurocopter_EC130 "Eurocopter EC130")[crashed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Orbic_Air_Eurocopter_EC130_crash "2024 Orbic Air Eurocopter EC130 crash"), killing all six occupants, including Nigerian banker [Herbert Wigwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Wigwe "Herbert Wigwe").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-18)11 February The [United States Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice") seized a [Boeing 747-300](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_747 "Boeing 747") registered as YV3531 belonging to Venezuelan state-owned airline [Emtrasur Cargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emtrasur_Cargo "Emtrasur Cargo"). The DOJ said that the aircraft was sold to Emtrasur Cargo by [Mahan Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahan_Air "Mahan Air"),[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-AP_US_Seizes_747-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-Ch-aviation_US_DOJ-20) a sanctioned Iranian airline due to its affiliation with the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_Revolutionary_Guard_Corps "Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps"),[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-21) which was in violation of American export control laws. The aircraft was initially detained by Argentina on 6 June 2022, shortly after the United States had issued a seizure warrant.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-AP_US_Seizes_747-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-Ch-aviation_US_DOJ-20) The aircraft was subsequently scrapped at [Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dade-Collier_Training_and_Transition_Airport "Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-23)18 February[Air Serbia Flight 324](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Serbia_Flight_324 "Air Serbia Flight 324"), an [Embraer 195](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embraer_195 "Embraer 195") operated by [Marathon Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_Airlines "Marathon Airlines"), struck landing lights on takeoff at Belgrade [Nikola Tesla Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikola_Tesla_Airport "Nikola Tesla Airport"). The aircraft flew for another hour before making an [emergency landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_landing "Emergency landing") at the same airport with a gaping hole in the [fuselage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuselage "Fuselage"). All 111 occupants were reported safe.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-25)20–25 February The [Singapore Airshow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore_Airshow "Singapore Airshow") was held.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-26) Highlights included orders for Airbus from [Vietjet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietjet "Vietjet") (20 [A330neos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A330neo "A330neo")) and [Starlux Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starlux_Airlines "Starlux Airlines") (three A330neos and five [A350Fs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A350#A350-1000F "A350")), Boeing from [Thai Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_Airways_International "Thai Airways International") (45 [787-9s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/787-9 "787-9")) and [Royal Brunei Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Brunei_Airlines "Royal Brunei Airlines") (four 787-9s), and Comac from [Tibet Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet_Airlines "Tibet Airlines") (40 [C919s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C919 "C919") and 10 [ARJ21s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARJ21 "ARJ21")).[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-27)21 February The [TAI TF Kaan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TAI_TF_Kaan "TAI TF Kaan"), a fifth-gen stealth fighter being developed by [Turkish Aerospace Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_Aerospace_Industries "Turkish Aerospace Industries"), performed its maiden flight.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-auto2-28)26 February[Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian "Canadian") Budget airline [Lynx Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynx_Air "Lynx Air") ceased operations due to financial issues.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-cease-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-auto6-30)

### March

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_aviation&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: March")]

5 March A [Dash 8-300](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DHC-8-300 "DHC-8-300") operating as [Safarilink Aviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safarilink_Aviation "Safarilink Aviation") Flight 53 from [Wilson Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Airport "Wilson Airport"), Nairobi to [Diani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukunda_Airport "Ukunda Airport") near [Mombasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombasa "Mombasa") was involved in a [mid-air collision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safarilink_Aviation_Flight_053 "Safarilink Aviation Flight 053") with a [Cessna 172](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cessna_172 "Cessna 172") operated by a local flying school. The Dash returned to Wilson and landed safely with no injuries among the 39 passengers and 5 crew. The Cessna crashed in [Nairobi National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi_National_Park "Nairobi National Park") killing the two occupants.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-31)8 March[David E.
