2 October A bomb that was dropped by [US Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Armed_Forces "United States Armed Forces") during World War II exploded under a taxiway at [Miyazaki Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miyazaki_Airport "Miyazaki Airport"), damaging the surface and disrupting operations.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-90)21 October An [Ilyushin Il-76](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilyushin_Il-76 "Ilyushin Il-76") is [shot down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_New_Way_Cargo_Airlines_Ilyushin_Il-76_shootdown "2024 New Way Cargo Airlines Ilyushin Il-76 shootdown") over [Darfur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darfur "Darfur"), Sudan, by the paramilitary [Rapid Support Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_Support_Forces "Rapid Support Forces"). All five occupants are killed in the subsequent crash.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-91)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-92)26 October After nearly 101 years of operation, [Czech Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_Airlines "Czech Airlines") ceases operations and becomes a holding company under its parent company [Smartwings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smartwings "Smartwings").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-auto3-93)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-auto7-94)30 October[Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberia_(airline) "Iberia (airline)"), the flag carrier of [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), takes delivery of the first [Airbus A321XLR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airbus_A321neo#A321XLR "Airbus A321neo") as the launch customer for the type. Registered as EC-OIL, this is the first out of eight A321XLRs ordered by Iberia.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-95)

### November

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_aviation&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: November")]

9 November[Total Linhas Aéreas Flight 5682](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_Linhas_A%C3%A9reas_Flight_5682 "Total Linhas Aéreas Flight 5682"), a [Boeing 737-4Q8 (SF)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_737-400 "Boeing 737-400"), [caught fire in flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In-flight_fire "In-flight fire"). The aircraft executed an [emergency landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_landing "Emergency landing") at [São Paulo/Guarulhos International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Paulo/Guarulhos_International_Airport "São Paulo/Guarulhos International Airport"), [São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Paulo "São Paulo"), Brazil, with both occupants surviving without injuries. The aircraft was delivered to the airline on 30 October.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-100)18 November[Spirit Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_Airlines "Spirit Airlines") files for [Chapter 11 bankruptcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapter_11_bankruptcy "Chapter 11 bankruptcy") protection due to losses, debt, competition and failed mergers.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-101)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-102)25 November A [Boeing 737-400(SF)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_737_Classic "Boeing 737 Classic") operating as [Swiftair Flight 5960](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swiftair_Flight_5960 "Swiftair Flight 5960"), from [Leipzig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leipzig/Halle_Airport "Leipzig/Halle Airport"), Germany, to [Vilnius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilnius_Airport "Vilnius Airport"), Lithuania, on behalf of [DHL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DHL "DHL"), crashed near a house on approach to Vilnius. One crew member was killed; no casualties were reported on the ground.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-103)26–28 November Following the opening of the expansion projects at [Nuuk Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuuk_Airport "Nuuk Airport"), the bulk of [Air Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Greenland "Air Greenland")'s services were transferred from [Kangerlussuaq Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangerlussuaq_Airport "Kangerlussuaq Airport") to Nuuk. ### December

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_aviation&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: December")]

13 December Following the identification of serious safety concerns, the [European Union Aviation Safety Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union_Aviation_Safety_Agency "European Union Aviation Safety Agency") (EASA) formally blacklisted [Air Tanzania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Tanzania "Air Tanzania") from operating to and within the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") (EU), denying the airline a third-country operator authorization (TCO),[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-110)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-111) a requirement for foreign airlines seeking to operate within the EU.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-112)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-113)20 December The [Government of Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Malaysia "Government of Malaysia") provisionally agreed to accept a second "no find, no fee" proposal from [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas")-based company [Ocean Infinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_Infinity "Ocean Infinity") to continue searching for the wreckage of [Malaysia Airlines Flight 370](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia_Airlines_Flight_370 "Malaysia Airlines Flight 370") in a new 15,000 square kilometres (5,800 sq mi) site in the [Indian Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Ocean "Indian Ocean"), which was based on new information and data analysis. If the wreckage found is considered to be substantive, Ocean Infinity would receive [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")70 million. Speaking at a press conference, [Transport minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Transport_(Malaysia) "Minister of Transport (Malaysia)")[Anthony Loke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Loke "Anthony Loke") stated, "We hope this time will be positive, that the wreckage will be found and give closure to the families."[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-114)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-115)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-116)[Turkish Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_Airlines "Turkish Airlines") was awarded a [Guinness World Record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_World_Record "Guinness World Record") for the most countries flown to by an airline, a record held by the airline since 2012. The award was presented in [Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile "Chile"), following Turkish Airlines' inaugural flight to [Arturo Merino Benítez International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Merino_Ben%C3%ADtez_International_Airport "Arturo Merino Benítez International Airport") in [Santiago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiago "Santiago"). Turkish Airlines now operates in 131 countries, 120 of them being confirmed as active by _Guinness World Records_.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-117)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-118)22 December A [Piper PA-42 Cheyenne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piper_PA-42_Cheyenne "Piper PA-42 Cheyenne")[crashed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Gramado_Piper_PA-42_crash "2024 Gramado Piper PA-42 crash") shortly after takeoff at [Canela Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canela_Airport "Canela Airport"), Brazil, killing all 10 occupants onboard and injuring a further 17 on the ground.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-119)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-120)23 December[Swiss International Air Lines Flight 1885](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swiss_International_Air_Lines_Flight_1885 "Swiss International Air Lines Flight 1885"), an [Airbus A220](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airbus_A220 "Airbus A220"), flying from [Bucharest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Coanda_International_Airport "Henri Coanda International Airport") to [Zurich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zurich_Airport "Zurich Airport"), diverted to [Graz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graz_Airport "Graz Airport") after smoke developed in the cabin was in cruise flight at 40,000 feet (FL400). The aircraft was evacuated using the [emergency slides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evacuation_slide "Evacuation slide"), and of the 79 people on board, 1 crew member died in the hospital.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-121) An engine failure due to a previously unknown fault pattern was flagged during initial investigations.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-122)25 December[Azerbaijan Airlines Flight 8243](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azerbaijan_Airlines_Flight_8243 "Azerbaijan Airlines Flight 8243"), an [Embraer E-190AR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embraer_190AR "Embraer 190AR"), was struck by a Russian surface-to-air missile and crashed near [Aktau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aktau "Aktau"), Kazakhstan, killing 38 of the 67 occupants onboard.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-123)28 December The [Philippine Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Air_Force "Philippine Air Force") withdrew the [North American OV-10 Bronco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_OV-10_Bronco "North American OV-10 Bronco") from its fleet, the last air force employing them.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-ret-124)29 December[Jeju Air Flight 2216](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeju_Air_Flight_2216 "Jeju Air Flight 2216"), a [Boeing 737-800](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_737-800 "Boeing 737-800"), overran the runway at [Muan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muan_International_Airport "Muan International Airport"), South Korea, and crashed while attempting to [belly land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belly_landing "Belly landing"). Out of the 181 occupants, 179 were killed; however 2 flight attendants seated at the rear of the plane survived.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-ap120d-125)30 December[Silver Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Airways "Silver Airways") filed for [Chapter 11 bankruptcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapter_11_bankruptcy "Chapter 11 bankruptcy") protection due to losses and debt.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-126)

## Aviation safety

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_aviation&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Aviation safety")]

In 2015, the all-accident rate was equal to 1.75 per one million flights; in 2024, this number decreased to 1.13. Compared to 2023 in which there were 72 onboard fatalities, 2024 experienced seven fatal commercial accidents and recorded a significant increase of onboard fatalities including 244 onboard deaths with 7 other deaths listed as "other". The surge in fatalities was linked to the crash of [Jeju Air Flight 2216](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeju_Air_Flight_2216 "Jeju Air Flight 2216") in December 2024.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPriyadarshiKhareUpmanMandal20255-128)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIATA20256-129) 2024 marked the deadliest year in commercial aviation since 2018.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-130)

In 2024, the [International Air Transport Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Air_Transport_Association "International Air Transport Association") (IATA) recorded over 430,000 cases of [GNSS jamming and spoofing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GNSS_jamming "GNSS jamming"). Most of the recorded cases occurred around conflict zones and were mostly related to military activities.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPriyadarshiKhareUpmanMandal20255-128)

## Deadliest crash

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2024_in_aviation&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Deadliest crash")]

The deadliest crash in 2024 occurred when [Jeju Air Flight 2216](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeju_Air_Flight_2216 "Jeju Air Flight 2216"), a [Boeing 737-800](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_737-800 "Boeing 737-800"), [overran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runway_excursion "Runway excursion") the runway while performing a [belly landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belly_landing "Belly landing") in [Muan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muan_International_Airport "Muan International Airport"), South Korea, on 29 December, killing 179 of the 181 passengers and crew on board.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_aviation#cite_note-131)

Q. What issue or issues do you believe are
most important to WSBA members right
now? How do you plan to address their
concerns?
A. Historically, WSBA members’ license fees
have been a consistent source of sensitiv-
ity and controversy. I believe that WSBA
members are wary of any increases to their
license fees. I was very proud that the Board
of Governors in the fall of 2020 pledged
not to increase WSBA member license fees
through 2026. I’ve worked hard to try to
honor that pledge while a governor.
I addressed the concern about license
fee increases by working hard for two
years as WSBA treasurer to help end each
fiscal year with significant increases to the
WSBA general fund, a result that is key to
avoiding the need for increasing license
fees. Going forward, this will also allow the
organization to have some flexibility in its
decision on what to do with the expiring
office building lease at the end of 2026. I
personally believe that the WSBA would be
best served by greatly downsizing its cur-
rent office space and looking to establish
small regional offices throughout the state,
rather than maintaining one large office in
downtown Seattle.

Q. What issue or issues do you believe are
most important to WSBA members right
now? How do you plan to address their
concerns?
A. Historically, WSBA members’ license fees
have been a consistent source of sensitiv-
ity and controversy. I believe that WSBA
members are wary of any increases to their
license fees. I was very proud that the Board
of Governors in the fall of 2020 pledged
not to increase WSBA member license fees
through 2026. I’ve worked hard to try to
honor that pledge while a governor.
I addressed the concern about license
fee increases by working hard for two
years as WSBA treasurer to help end each
fiscal year with significant increases to the
WSBA general fund, a result that is key to
avoiding the need for increasing license
fees. Going forward, this will also allow the
organization to have some flexibility in its
decision on what to do with the expiring
office building lease at the end of 2026. I
personally believe that the WSBA would be
best served by greatly downsizing its cur-
rent office space and looking to establish
small regional offices throughout the state,
rather than maintaining one large office in
downtown Seattle.

ant issues of concern to the public.

by “legal deserts” in parts of the state) is the

members are wary of any increases to their
license fees. I was very proud that the Board
of Governors in the fall of 2020 pledged

fiscal year with significant increases to the

office building lease at the end of 2026. I
personally believe that the WSBA would be

rent office space and looking to establish
small regional offices throughout the state,

downtown Seattle.

Q. What issue or issues do you believe are
most important to WSBA members right
now? How do you plan to address their
concerns?
A. Historically, WSBA members’ license fees
have been a consistent source of sensitiv-
ity and controversy. I believe that WSBA
members are wary of any increases to their
license fees. I was very proud that the Board
of Governors in the fall of 2020 pledged
not to increase WSBA member license fees
through 2026. I’ve worked hard to try to
honor that pledge while a governor.
I addressed the concern about license
fee increases by working hard for two
years as WSBA treasurer to help end each
fiscal year with significant increases to the
WSBA general fund, a result that is key to
avoiding the need for increasing license
fees. Going forward, this will also allow the
organization to have some flexibility in its
decision on what to do with the expiring
office building lease at the end of 2026. I
personally believe that the WSBA would be
best served by greatly downsizing its cur-
rent office space and looking to establish
small regional offices throughout the state,
rather than maintaining one large office in
downtown Seattle.

# F35B Fighter Jet crashes near Albuquerque International Sunport

[](https://www.kirtland.af.mil/DesktopModules/ArticleCS/Print.aspx?PortalId=52&ModuleId=65883&Article=3803170)[](mailto:?Subject=F35B%20Fighter%20Jet%20crashes%20near%20Albuquerque%20International%20Sunport%20-%20Kirtland%20Air%20Force%20Base&body=Here%20is%20an%20article%20I%20think%20you%20will%20find%20interesting:%20https://www.kirtland.af.mil/News/Article-Display/Article/3803170/f35b-fighter-jet-crashes-near-albuquerque-international-sunport/)

*   Published June 11, 2024
*    By Allen Winston 
*   377th Air Base Wing Public Affairs

**KIRTLAND AIR FORCE BASE, N.M. --**
An F-35B aircraft was involved in a crash southwest of the Kirtland, at 1:48 p.m., May 28, 2024.  
  
 The U.S. Air Force pilot ferrying the aircraft departed from the Lockheed Martin facility at Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base, Fort Worth, Texas, that morning, and landed at Kirtland at 1 p.m. to refuel. Shortly after takeoff for Edwards Air Force Base, Calif., the aircraft crashed on University Blvd SE, just north of Rio Bravo Blvd SE, where it was consumed by fire.  
  
 The pilot, assigned to the Defense Contract Management Agency, successfully ejected at a low altitude from the aircraft before the crash. He was triaged on scene and transported to University of New Mexico Hospital where he underwent surgery for his injuries. He remains in serious, but stable condition.  
  
 Bernalillo County Fire Rescue were the first to arrive on scene and began search and rescue of the pilot as well as fire suppression measures to put out the fire from the immediate aircraft and the surrounding landscape. They were quickly joined by Battalion One Albuquerque Fire and Rescue and Kirtland AFB Fire Department. Emergency responders secured the scene and ensured the safety of the area.  
  
 A combined resilient team was immediately evident as military agencies, city agencies, and the local community rallied together. The coordination and rapid response showcased the strength and collaboration between county, city and installation sectors. Together, they established a command center, rescued the pilot, rapidly contained the fire and secured the scene.  
  
 The Kirtland Partnership Committee has been closely working with the pilot’s family to create a sense of community and comfort during this trying time, offering support and delivering a care package during their stay. “As a community, we are grateful to have such a capable and well-trained team in New Mexico to overcome these events,” said Megan DeLaRosa, Kirtland Partnership Committee Director.  
  
 One thing is clear-- training and teamwork pay off. Everyone knew their role and pulled together seamlessly for this mission. Col. Michael Power, 377th Air Base Wing and Kirtland Air Force Base installation commander remarked on the incredible interagency teamwork and immediate response to the crash.  
  
 “The last eight days has seen Team Kirtland come together to support the pilot and community as a result of the recent F-35 crash,” Power said. “The 377th Air Base Wing, 58th and 150th Special Operations Wings, as well as first responders of Bernalillo County, the city of Albuquerque, and so many more came together to provide immeasurable support during this incident.”  
  
 The Navy Region Southeast On-scene Coordinator program, whose mission is to provide emergency response and consequence management services for all Navy and U.S. Marine Corps incidents that may have an environmental or public health impact, arrived from Naval Air Station Jacksonville, Fla., on June 1. They immediately began working on the recovery and removal of the aircraft wreckage. The program is also responsible for ensuring that all restoration of the area aligns with environmental laws.  
  
 “The leaders and team at Kirtland Air Force Base did an excellent job stabilizing the site and preparing to receive our team,” explained John Baxter, Federal On-scene Coordinator. “Once we assumed command, we continued to work closely with installation leaders, stakeholders, and investigators to remove the debris and minimize further disruptions to the local community.”  
  
 A Navy team has been assigned to the cleanup of the site. The clean-up and relocation of the aircraft is expected to take days not weeks. Local officials are working with the City of Albuquerque and the Office of Emergency Management to mitigate disruption in traffic on the roads near the crash site.  
  
 The cause of the crash is still under investigation and being reviewed by an Air Force Interim Safety Board, NTSB, and led by the Navy.

# F35B Fighter Jet crashes near Albuquerque International Sunport

[](https://www.kirtland.af.mil/DesktopModules/ArticleCS/Print.aspx?PortalId=52&ModuleId=65883&Article=3803170)[](mailto:?Subject=F35B%20Fighter%20Jet%20crashes%20near%20Albuquerque%20International%20Sunport%20-%20Kirtland%20Air%20Force%20Base&body=Here%20is%20an%20article%20I%20think%20you%20will%20find%20interesting:%20https://www.kirtland.af.mil/News/Article-Display/Article/3803170/f35b-fighter-jet-crashes-near-albuquerque-international-sunport/)

*   Published June 11, 2024
*    By Allen Winston 
*   377th Air Base Wing Public Affairs

**KIRTLAND AIR FORCE BASE, N.M. --**
An F-35B aircraft was involved in a crash southwest of the Kirtland, at 1:48 p.m., May 28, 2024.  
  
 The U.S. Air Force pilot ferrying the aircraft departed from the Lockheed Martin facility at Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base, Fort Worth, Texas, that morning, and landed at Kirtland at 1 p.m. to refuel. Shortly after takeoff for Edwards Air Force Base, Calif., the aircraft crashed on University Blvd SE, just north of Rio Bravo Blvd SE, where it was consumed by fire.  
  
 The pilot, assigned to the Defense Contract Management Agency, successfully ejected at a low altitude from the aircraft before the crash. He was triaged on scene and transported to University of New Mexico Hospital where he underwent surgery for his injuries. He remains in serious, but stable condition.  
  
 Bernalillo County Fire Rescue were the first to arrive on scene and began search and rescue of the pilot as well as fire suppression measures to put out the fire from the immediate aircraft and the surrounding landscape. They were quickly joined by Battalion One Albuquerque Fire and Rescue and Kirtland AFB Fire Department. Emergency responders secured the scene and ensured the safety of the area.  
  
 A combined resilient team was immediately evident as military agencies, city agencies, and the local community rallied together. The coordination and rapid response showcased the strength and collaboration between county, city and installation sectors. Together, they established a command center, rescued the pilot, rapidly contained the fire and secured the scene.  
  
 The Kirtland Partnership Committee has been closely working with the pilot’s family to create a sense of community and comfort during this trying time, offering support and delivering a care package during their stay. “As a community, we are grateful to have such a capable and well-trained team in New Mexico to overcome these events,” said Megan DeLaRosa, Kirtland Partnership Committee Director.  
  
 One thing is clear-- training and teamwork pay off. Everyone knew their role and pulled together seamlessly for this mission. Col. Michael Power, 377th Air Base Wing and Kirtland Air Force Base installation commander remarked on the incredible interagency teamwork and immediate response to the crash.  
  
 “The last eight days has seen Team Kirtland come together to support the pilot and community as a result of the recent F-35 crash,” Power said. “The 377th Air Base Wing, 58th and 150th Special Operations Wings, as well as first responders of Bernalillo County, the city of Albuquerque, and so many more came together to provide immeasurable support during this incident.”  
  
 The Navy Region Southeast On-scene Coordinator program, whose mission is to provide emergency response and consequence management services for all Navy and U.S. Marine Corps incidents that may have an environmental or public health impact, arrived from Naval Air Station Jacksonville, Fla., on June 1. They immediately began working on the recovery and removal of the aircraft wreckage. The program is also responsible for ensuring that all restoration of the area aligns with environmental laws.  
  
 “The leaders and team at Kirtland Air Force Base did an excellent job stabilizing the site and preparing to receive our team,” explained John Baxter, Federal On-scene Coordinator. “Once we assumed command, we continued to work closely with installation leaders, stakeholders, and investigators to remove the debris and minimize further disruptions to the local community.”  
  
 A Navy team has been assigned to the cleanup of the site. The clean-up and relocation of the aircraft is expected to take days not weeks. Local officials are working with the City of Albuquerque and the Office of Emergency Management to mitigate disruption in traffic on the roads near the crash site.  
  
 The cause of the crash is still under investigation and being reviewed by an Air Force Interim Safety Board, NTSB, and led by the Navy.

The F-35 crash on May 28, 2024 was one of the most significant events of the year. Here is a video we put together about the response and news coverage of the event. This plane crash resulted in a large, multi-agency response and national news coverage. Bernalillo County Fire, Albuquerque Fire and Kirtland AFB FD all responded. The pilot suffered serious injuries and was transported by Rescue 1 to the hospital. No other injuries were reported but responders were monitored following the crash due to the nature of the aircraft. This concludes the look back at significant events of 2024. It was another very busy year for AFR. Thank you all for following along and thank you for the continued support. #albuquerque #abqfirerescue

The F-35 crash on May 28, 2024 was one of the most significant events of the year. Here is a video we put together about the response and news coverage of the event. This plane crash resulted in a large, multi-agency response and national news coverage. Bernalillo County Fire, Albuquerque Fire and Kirtland AFB FD all responded. The pilot suffered serious injuries and was transported by Rescue 1 to the hospital. No other injuries were reported but responders were monitored following the crash due to the nature of the aircraft. This concludes the look back at significant events of 2024. It was another very busy year for AFR. Thank you all for following along and thank you for the continued support. #albuquerque #abqfirerescue

# [Updated] F-35B Crashes Near Albuquerque Airport, New Mexico

Published on: May 28, 2024 at 11:56 PM CEST

![Image 6: David Cenciotti](blob:http://localhost/f0128c60610137008f59e4190a7b43cc)[David Cenciotti](https://theaviationist.com/author/cencio4/)

![Image 8: F-35 crash](https://theaviationist.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/F-35-crash-860x484.jpg)

## An F-35 crashed near Albuquerque International. According to the first reports, the pilot successfully ejected.

An F-35 Lightning II aircraft has crashed near Albuquerque International Sunport (ABQ), New Mexico, on May 28, 2024. Images showing the explosion the emergency team trying to extinguish the fire at the crash site have started circulating online.

> I just witnessed a major, horrific aircraft crash with an explosion and dust rising into the air while I’m on my flight on the runway. I will report on it soon, waiting for more details but the person behind me said it was possible it was a helicopter or some type of single… [pic.twitter.com/NA8pQVdV6W](https://t.co/NA8pQVdV6W)
> 
> 
> — R A W S A L E R T S (@rawsalerts) [May 28, 2024](https://twitter.com/rawsalerts/status/1795546729611489584?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

> [#BREAKING](https://twitter.com/hashtag/BREAKING?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw) A F-35 fighter jet just crashed during takeoff at Albuquerque International, New Mexico.
> 
> 
> Pilot reportedly ejected. [pic.twitter.com/eAFSmgWJ00](https://t.co/eAFSmgWJ00)
> 
> 
> — Clash Report (@clashreport) [May 28, 2024](https://twitter.com/clashreport/status/1795554760042446908?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

According to [KOB4](https://www.kob.com/new-mexico/crews-responding-to-military-aircraft-crash-near-university-and-rio-bravo/), the pilot would be conscious and breathing and has been taken to the hospital.

The F-35 had just taken off from Runway 21 at ABQ.

> F-35 mishap at Albuquerque? Audio via [@liveatc](https://twitter.com/liveatc?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)[https://t.co/8E9eu1HHhn](https://t.co/8E9eu1HHhn)[pic.twitter.com/wnYAHt4OwR](https://t.co/wnYAHt4OwR)
> 
> 
> — Thenewarea51 (@thenewarea51) [May 28, 2024](https://twitter.com/thenewarea51/status/1795552433482960948?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

Although it’s too early to say, by the look of the wreckage, it looks like the type was an F-35B (to be confirmed).

### Previous crashes

The most recent crash of a U.S. F-35 occurred on Sept. 17, 2023, when a U.S. Marine Corps F-35B crashed in South Carolina after the pilot ejected [due to a malfunction](https://theaviationist.com/2023/09/18/missing-f-35b/). The aircraft continued flying for about 60 miles before crashing in a field near Indiantown, South Carolina. The incident led to a day-long search for the wreckage, which was eventually [found in a field](https://theaviationist.com/2023/09/19/missing-f-35b-found-in-field/).

Previously, on Dec. 15, 2022, an F-35B crashed [during a vertical landing](https://theaviationist.com/2022/12/15/f-35b-crash-at-fort-worth/) at Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth in Texas. The F-35B involved in that crash was Lockheed-owned (hence not yet delivered to/accepted by the final customer).

_This is developing story, we will update it as soon as new details emerge._

_Update May 29, 2024 05.00 GMT_

The F-35B had departed from Lockheed Martin’s Manufacturing Plant in Fort Worth, Texas and was heading to Edwards Air Force Base in California via a fuel stopover at Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico. It crashed shortly after take off from Kirtland AFB.

> According the Lockheed Martin, the F-35 which Crashed earlier today near Albuquerque International Sunport in New Mexico was actually a F-35B Variant instead of what was previously believed to be an “A” Variant, meaning this Aircraft was likely meant for the U.S. Marine Corps not…

> 
> — OSINTdefender (@sentdefender) [May 28, 2024](https://twitter.com/sentdefender/status/1795596827938427355?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

According to some unverified accounts circulating online, on departure, the F-35B was offered by the ATC a rapid climb to 20,000 feet, but the pilot responded that he promised to do a short take off for some guys on the ramp. Indeed, the images of the crash show the F-35B taking off in STOVL mode.

## An F-35 crashed near Albuquerque International. According to the first reports, the pilot successfully ejected.

An F-35 Lightning II aircraft has crashed near Albuquerque International Sunport (ABQ), New Mexico, on May 28, 2024. Images showing the explosion the emergency team trying to extinguish the fire at the crash site have started circulating online.

> I just witnessed a major, horrific aircraft crash with an explosion and dust rising into the air while I’m on my flight on the runway. I will report on it soon, waiting for more details but the person behind me said it was possible it was a helicopter or some type of single… [pic.twitter.com/NA8pQVdV6W](https://t.co/NA8pQVdV6W)
> 
> 
> — R A W S A L E R T S (@rawsalerts) [May 28, 2024](https://twitter.com/rawsalerts/status/1795546729611489584?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

> [#BREAKING](https://twitter.com/hashtag/BREAKING?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw) A F-35 fighter jet just crashed during takeoff at Albuquerque International, New Mexico.
> 
> 
> Pilot reportedly ejected. [pic.twitter.com/eAFSmgWJ00](https://t.co/eAFSmgWJ00)
> 
> 
> — Clash Report (@clashreport) [May 28, 2024](https://twitter.com/clashreport/status/1795554760042446908?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

According to [KOB4](https://www.kob.com/new-mexico/crews-responding-to-military-aircraft-crash-near-university-and-rio-bravo/), the pilot would be conscious and breathing and has been taken to the hospital.

The F-35 had just taken off from Runway 21 at ABQ.

> F-35 mishap at Albuquerque? Audio via [@liveatc](https://twitter.com/liveatc?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)[https://t.co/8E9eu1HHhn](https://t.co/8E9eu1HHhn)[pic.twitter.com/wnYAHt4OwR](https://t.co/wnYAHt4OwR)
> 
> 
> — Thenewarea51 (@thenewarea51) [May 28, 2024](https://twitter.com/thenewarea51/status/1795552433482960948?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

Although it’s too early to say, by the look of the wreckage, it looks like the type was an F-35B (to be confirmed).

### Previous crashes

The most recent crash of a U.S. F-35 occurred on Sept. 17, 2023, when a U.S. Marine Corps F-35B crashed in South Carolina after the pilot ejected [due to a malfunction](https://theaviationist.com/2023/09/18/missing-f-35b/). The aircraft continued flying for about 60 miles before crashing in a field near Indiantown, South Carolina. The incident led to a day-long search for the wreckage, which was eventually [found in a field](https://theaviationist.com/2023/09/19/missing-f-35b-found-in-field/).

Previously, on Dec. 15, 2022, an F-35B crashed [during a vertical landing](https://theaviationist.com/2022/12/15/f-35b-crash-at-fort-worth/) at Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth in Texas. The F-35B involved in that crash was Lockheed-owned (hence not yet delivered to/accepted by the final customer).

_This is developing story, we will update it as soon as new details emerge._

# F-35B Crash On Take Off From Kirtland AFB Caught On Camera

Published on: May 30, 2024 at 11:18 PM CEST

![Image 6: David Cenciotti](blob:http://localhost/f0128c60610137008f59e4190a7b43cc)[David Cenciotti](https://theaviationist.com/author/cencio4/)

![Image 8: F-35B crash](https://theaviationist.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/F-35B-crash-top-new-860x484.jpg)

The F-35B about to crash following pilot's ejection (Image courtesy: Alex McCready)

SHARE

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Ftheaviationist.com%2F2024%2F05%2F30%2Ff-35b-crash-on-take-off-from-kirtland-afb-caught-on-camera%2F)[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=F-35B+Crash+On+Take+Off+From+Kirtland+AFB+Caught+On+Camera&url=https%3A%2F%2Ftheaviationist.com%2F2024%2F05%2F30%2Ff-35b-crash-on-take-off-from-kirtland-afb-caught-on-camera%2F&via=cencio4)[](javascript:if(window.print)window.print())

## We have obtained some interesting photographs showing the moments the F-35B Lightning II crashed near Albuquerque.

The F-35B that crashed on May 28, 2024, in New Mexico was piloted by an Air Force pilot, according to statements from the F-35 Joint Program Office and the Air Force. The pilot ejected at a low altitude and sustained serious injuries but is currently in stable condition.

The Air Force pilot was flying the jet on behalf of the Defense Contract Management Agency.

The F-35B had originally departed from Lockheed Martin’s Manufacturing Plant in Fort Worth, Texas, and was en route to Edwards Air Force Base in California, with a refueling stop planned at Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico. The crash occurred shortly after its departure from Kirtland AFB. The incident happened at 1:48 pm local time, just outside the fenced boundary of the Albuquerque International Sunport/Kirtland Air Force Base.

Some unverified online reports suggest that upon departure, the air traffic control offered the F-35B a rapid ascent to 20,000 feet, but the pilot declined, stating he had promised to perform a short takeoff for observers on the ramp.

Indeed, crash images show the aircraft taking off in Short Takeoff and Vertical Landing (STOVL) mode: images of the aircraft taken just before the crash and shared on social media show it in a nose-high position for a STOVL takeoff, kicking up considerable dust on the runway overrun. The aircraft was in full STOVL configuration, with the dorsal lift fan door open, engine exhaust ventral doors open, and elevons fully deflected.

Alex McCready took a couple of live shots with her iPhone of the F-35B. Since Live Photos feature records what happens 1.5 seconds before and after you take a picture, the images provide a pretty clear view (from distance) of the incident: you can see the aircraft at very low altitude moments before the pilot ejected.

[![Image 9](blob:http://localhost/50f2916e9271a8c4c511dad627489e13)](https://theaviationist.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/F-35B-crash-top.jpg)

The F-35B nose high, about to hit the ground. (Image courtesy: Alex McCready)

Then, after the ejection the aircraft continued to fly for some hundred meters before crashing into the ground.

[![Image 11: F-35B crash](blob:http://localhost/65bdfc46a3cb6317bcf5d8af66257ee7)](https://theaviationist.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/F-35B-crash-top-new.jpg)

The F-35B about to crash following pilot’s ejection (Image courtesy: Alex McCready)

Here are the Live Photos that, together, provide an interesting look at the incident.

> The moment the F-35B crashed on takeoff from Kirtland AFB, NM, was caught on camera by Alex McCready ([@lexlynn505](https://twitter.com/lexlynn505?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)) who shared the live photos with us. We can see the pilot ejecting as the aircraft was extremely low. After the ejection the F-35B continued to fly before crashing.… [pic.twitter.com/jnUrejqTPS](https://t.co/jnUrejqTPS)
> 
> 
> — The Aviationist (@TheAviationist) [May 30, 2024](https://twitter.com/TheAviationist/status/1796270564253774243?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

The aircraft that crashed on May 29 was a Technology Refresh 2-configured F-35, delivered in September 2023. It was one of the last TR-2s built due to delays in TR-3 testing. The jet, owned by the U.S. government and piloted by a government pilot, was being transferred from Fort Worth, Texas, to Edwards Air Force Base, California, for modifications and testing, with a refueling stop at Kirtland AFB. The cause of the crash is under review by an Air Force Interim Safety Board.

# F-35B Crash On Take Off From Kirtland AFB Caught On Camera

Published on: May 30, 2024 at 11:18 PM CEST

![Image 6: David Cenciotti](blob:http://localhost/f0128c60610137008f59e4190a7b43cc)[David Cenciotti](https://theaviationist.com/author/cencio4/)

![Image 8: F-35B crash](https://theaviationist.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/F-35B-crash-top-new-860x484.jpg)

The F-35B about to crash following pilot's ejection (Image courtesy: Alex McCready)

## We have obtained some interesting photographs showing the moments the F-35B Lightning II crashed near Albuquerque.

The F-35B that crashed on May 28, 2024, in New Mexico was piloted by an Air Force pilot, according to statements from the F-35 Joint Program Office and the Air Force. The pilot ejected at a low altitude and sustained serious injuries but is currently in stable condition.

The Air Force pilot was flying the jet on behalf of the Defense Contract Management Agency.

The F-35B had originally departed from Lockheed Martin’s Manufacturing Plant in Fort Worth, Texas, and was en route to Edwards Air Force Base in California, with a refueling stop planned at Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico. The crash occurred shortly after its departure from Kirtland AFB. The incident happened at 1:48 pm local time, just outside the fenced boundary of the Albuquerque International Sunport/Kirtland Air Force Base.

Some unverified online reports suggest that upon departure, the air traffic control offered the F-35B a rapid ascent to 20,000 feet, but the pilot declined, stating he had promised to perform a short takeoff for observers on the ramp.

Indeed, crash images show the aircraft taking off in Short Takeoff and Vertical Landing (STOVL) mode: images of the aircraft taken just before the crash and shared on social media show it in a nose-high position for a STOVL takeoff, kicking up considerable dust on the runway overrun. The aircraft was in full STOVL configuration, with the dorsal lift fan door open, engine exhaust ventral doors open, and elevons fully deflected.

Alex McCready took a couple of live shots with her iPhone of the F-35B. Since Live Photos feature records what happens 1.5 seconds before and after you take a picture, the images provide a pretty clear view (from distance) of the incident: you can see the aircraft at very low altitude moments before the pilot ejected.

[![Image 9](blob:http://localhost/50f2916e9271a8c4c511dad627489e13)](https://theaviationist.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/F-35B-crash-top.jpg)

The F-35B nose high, about to hit the ground. (Image courtesy: Alex McCready)

Then, after the ejection the aircraft continued to fly for some hundred meters before crashing into the ground.

[![Image 11: F-35B crash](blob:http://localhost/65bdfc46a3cb6317bcf5d8af66257ee7)](https://theaviationist.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/F-35B-crash-top-new.jpg)

The F-35B about to crash following pilot’s ejection (Image courtesy: Alex McCready)

Here are the Live Photos that, together, provide an interesting look at the incident.

> The moment the F-35B crashed on takeoff from Kirtland AFB, NM, was caught on camera by Alex McCready ([@lexlynn505](https://twitter.com/lexlynn505?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)) who shared the live photos with us. We can see the pilot ejecting as the aircraft was extremely low. After the ejection the F-35B continued to fly before crashing.… [pic.twitter.com/jnUrejqTPS](https://t.co/jnUrejqTPS)
> 
> 
> — The Aviationist (@TheAviationist) [May 30, 2024](https://twitter.com/TheAviationist/status/1796270564253774243?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

The aircraft that crashed on May 29 was a Technology Refresh 2-configured F-35, delivered in September 2023. It was one of the last TR-2s built due to delays in TR-3 testing. The jet, owned by the U.S. government and piloted by a government pilot, was being transferred from Fort Worth, Texas, to Edwards Air Force Base, California, for modifications and testing, with a refueling stop at Kirtland AFB. The cause of the crash is under review by an Air Force Interim Safety Board.

An Air Force pilot was injured after ejecting from an F-35B jet, which crashed in Albuquerque, New Mexico on Tuesday, officials said.

The plane, which [costs a cool $135 million](https://armscontrolcenter.org/f-35-joint-strike-fighter-costs-challenges/), smashed into the ground just south of Albuquerque International Sunport around 1:50 p.m. after refueling at Kirtland Air Force Base, [according to KOB4](https://www.kob.com/new-mexico/military-aircraft-f-35b-crashes-near-university-rio-bravo-albuquerque/).

The pilot, the only person on board, ejected safely and was taken to the University of New Mexico hospital in stable condition, according to the city’s fire department and military officials.

The jet had been flying from a Lockheed Martin facility at the Naval Air Reserve Station in Fort Worth, Texas to Edwards Air Force Base in California when it crashed.

An Air Force pilot was injured after ejecting from an F-35B jet, which crashed in Albuquerque, New Mexico on Tuesday, officials said.

The plane, which [costs a cool $135 million](https://armscontrolcenter.org/f-35-joint-strike-fighter-costs-challenges/), smashed into the ground just south of Albuquerque International Sunport around 1:50 p.m. after refueling at Kirtland Air Force Base, [according to KOB4](https://www.kob.com/new-mexico/military-aircraft-f-35b-crashes-near-university-rio-bravo-albuquerque/).

The pilot, the only person on board, ejected safely and was taken to the University of New Mexico hospital in stable condition, according to the city’s fire department and military officials.

The jet had been flying from a Lockheed Martin facility at the Naval Air Reserve Station in Fort Worth, Texas to Edwards Air Force Base in California when it crashed.

Photos from the crash site show the scorched wreckage of the plane burning in a field by the side of a road.

# F-35B Fighter Jet Crashes Near Albuquerque International, Pilot Ejected

*   [SOFX Staff Writer](https://www.sofx.com/author/editor-sofx/)

[Share on Facebook](http://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sofx.com%2Ff-35b-fighter-jet-crashes-near-albuquerque-international-pilot-ejected%2F)[Share on Twitter](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=F-35B%20Fighter%20Jet%20Crashes%20Near%20Albuquerque%20International%2C%20Pilot%20Ejected&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sofx.com%2Ff-35b-fighter-jet-crashes-near-albuquerque-international-pilot-ejected%2F)[LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sofx.com%2Ff-35b-fighter-jet-crashes-near-albuquerque-international-pilot-ejected%2F&title=F-35B%20Fighter%20Jet%20Crashes%20Near%20Albuquerque%20International%2C%20Pilot%20Ejected)

An F-35B fighter jet crashed near Albuquerque International Sunport (ABQ), New Mexico, on May 28, 2024. The incident occurred shortly before 2 p.m. local time after the aircraft had taken off from Runway 21. The pilot successfully ejected and was taken to the hospital with serious injuries but was reported to be conscious and breathing.

The F-35B, a developmental test aircraft owned by Lockheed Martin, was en route from Fort Worth, Texas, to Edwards Air Force Base, California, when it made a refueling stop at Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico. According to Lockheed Martin, the aircraft crashed soon after resuming its flight. “Safety is our priority, and we will follow appropriate investigation protocol,” Lockheed Martin stated.

Albuquerque Fire Rescue Public Information Officer Lt. Jason Fejer confirmed that the pilot was transported to the hospital categorized as “red,” indicating serious injuries requiring immediate attention. Two civilians were also assessed at the scene; one refused treatment, while the other was a non-patient struck by debris.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has directed inquiries to the Marine Corps, given that the F-35B is a model used primarily by the Marine Corps. This particular aircraft type is designed for short take-off and vertical landing, making it unique among the F-35 variants, which include the F-35A used by the Air Force and the F-35C flown by both the Navy and Marine Corps.

Footage from the crash site showed emergency teams working to extinguish the fire caused by the crash. The aircraft, a single-seat model, had no other crew members on board. The cause of the crash remains under investigation.

The incident follows previous crashes involving F-35 aircraft. Notably, on September 17, 2023, a U.S. Marine Corps [F-35B crashed in South Carolina](https://www.sofx.com/marine-corps-f-35-crash-site-discovered-in-south-carolina/) after the pilot ejected due to a malfunction, and on December 15, 2022, an F-35B crashed during a vertical landing at Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth in Texas. Both incidents involved developmental models owned by Lockheed Martin.

The F-35 program has faced scrutiny over performance and cost issues. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) recently highlighted that the aircraft’s [mission-capable rate was about 55% as of March 2023](https://www.sofx.com/gao-report-highlights-unsustainable-f-35-repair-backlog/). Despite these challenges, the Pentagon plans to buy approximately 2,500 F-35s by the mid-2040s, with the program’s total cost estimated at $2 trillion for procurement and maintenance until the fleet’s planned retirement in 2088.

# F-35B Fighter Jet Crashes Near Albuquerque International, Pilot Ejected

*   [SOFX Staff Writer](https://www.sofx.com/author/editor-sofx/)
*   [May 29, 2024](https://www.sofx.com/2024/05/29/)

![Image 4](https://www.sofx.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/SI-1-33.jpg)

A U.S. Marine Corps F-35B Lightning II with Marine Fighter Attack Squadron 225, Marine Aircraft Group (MAG) 13, 3rd Marine Aircraft Wing, taxis into the flight-line towards a Forward Arming and Refueling Point at U.S. Army Yuma Proving Grounds, Yuma, Arizona, May 23, 2022. (U.S. Marine Corps photo by Sgt. Samuel Ruiz)

[Share on Facebook](http://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sofx.com%2Ff-35b-fighter-jet-crashes-near-albuquerque-international-pilot-ejected%2F)[Share on Twitter](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=F-35B%20Fighter%20Jet%20Crashes%20Near%20Albuquerque%20International%2C%20Pilot%20Ejected&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sofx.com%2Ff-35b-fighter-jet-crashes-near-albuquerque-international-pilot-ejected%2F)[LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sofx.com%2Ff-35b-fighter-jet-crashes-near-albuquerque-international-pilot-ejected%2F&title=F-35B%20Fighter%20Jet%20Crashes%20Near%20Albuquerque%20International%2C%20Pilot%20Ejected)

An F-35B fighter jet crashed near Albuquerque International Sunport (ABQ), New Mexico, on May 28, 2024. The incident occurred shortly before 2 p.m. local time after the aircraft had taken off from Runway 21. The pilot successfully ejected and was taken to the hospital with serious injuries but was reported to be conscious and breathing.

The F-35B, a developmental test aircraft owned by Lockheed Martin, was en route from Fort Worth, Texas, to Edwards Air Force Base, California, when it made a refueling stop at Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico. According to Lockheed Martin, the aircraft crashed soon after resuming its flight. “Safety is our priority, and we will follow appropriate investigation protocol,” Lockheed Martin stated.

Albuquerque Fire Rescue Public Information Officer Lt. Jason Fejer confirmed that the pilot was transported to the hospital categorized as “red,” indicating serious injuries requiring immediate attention. Two civilians were also assessed at the scene; one refused treatment, while the other was a non-patient struck by debris.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has directed inquiries to the Marine Corps, given that the F-35B is a model used primarily by the Marine Corps. This particular aircraft type is designed for short take-off and vertical landing, making it unique among the F-35 variants, which include the F-35A used by the Air Force and the F-35C flown by both the Navy and Marine Corps.

Footage from the crash site showed emergency teams working to extinguish the fire caused by the crash. The aircraft, a single-seat model, had no other crew members on board. The cause of the crash remains under investigation.

The incident follows previous crashes involving F-35 aircraft. Notably, on September 17, 2023, a U.S. Marine Corps [F-35B crashed in South Carolina](https://www.sofx.com/marine-corps-f-35-crash-site-discovered-in-south-carolina/) after the pilot ejected due to a malfunction, and on December 15, 2022, an F-35B crashed during a vertical landing at Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth in Texas. Both incidents involved developmental models owned by Lockheed Martin.

The F-35 program has faced scrutiny over performance and cost issues. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) recently highlighted that the aircraft’s [mission-capable rate was about 55% as of March 2023](https://www.sofx.com/gao-report-highlights-unsustainable-f-35-repair-backlog/). Despite these challenges, the Pentagon plans to buy approximately 2,500 F-35s by the mid-2040s, with the program’s total cost estimated at $2 trillion for procurement and maintenance until the fleet’s planned retirement in 2088.

An Air Force pilot was injured after ejecting from an F-35B jet, which crashed in Albuquerque, New Mexico on Tuesday, officials said.

The plane, which [costs a cool $135 million](https://armscontrolcenter.org/f-35-joint-strike-fighter-costs-challenges/), smashed into the ground just south of Albuquerque International Sunport around 1:50 p.m. after refueling at Kirtland Air Force Base, [according to KOB4](https://www.kob.com/new-mexico/military-aircraft-f-35b-crashes-near-university-rio-bravo-albuquerque/).

The pilot, the only person on board, ejected safely and was taken to the University of New Mexico hospital in stable condition, according to the city’s fire department and military officials.

The jet had been flying from a Lockheed Martin facility at the Naval Air Reserve Station in Fort Worth, Texas to Edwards Air Force Base in California when it crashed.

Photos from the crash site show the scorched wreckage of the plane burning in a field by the side of a road.

Kirtland Air Force Base is leading the investigation into the crash.

A base spokesperson told The Post that more information would be released as it becomes available.

It’s the second military plane crash in New Mexico in as many months. In April, an F-16 Fighting Falcon — which cost about $63 million each — went down in a remote area near the Holloman Air Force Base in the southern part of the state.

The pilot suffered minor injuries after he was also ejected from the plane.

Q. What issue or issues do you believe are
most important to WSBA members right
now? How do you plan to address their
concerns?
A. Historically, WSBA members’ license fees
have been a consistent source of sensitiv-
ity and controversy. I believe that WSBA
members are wary of any increases to their
license fees. I was very proud that the Board
of Governors in the fall of 2020 pledged
not to increase WSBA member license fees
through 2026. I’ve worked hard to try to
honor that pledge while a governor.
I addressed the concern about license
fee increases by working hard for two
years as WSBA treasurer to help end each
fiscal year with significant increases to the
WSBA general fund, a result that is key to
avoiding the need for increasing license
fees. Going forward, this will also allow the
organization to have some flexibility in its
decision on what to do with the expiring
office building lease at the end of 2026. I
personally believe that the WSBA would be
best served by greatly downsizing its cur-
rent office space and looking to establish
small regional offices throughout the state,
rather than maintaining one large office in
downtown Seattle.
